items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that קדשי קדשים slaughtered in the south, or with various other disqualifications, still incur מעילה. Rabbi Yehoshua gives a rule: anything that had a permitted time for priests does not incur מעילה, while anything that did not, does. Examples are given for each category.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that קדשי קדשים (most holy offerings) slaughtered in the south still incur מעילה (misappropriation).
The mishnah lists additional disqualifying scenarios (slaughter in south/receive in north, day/night, night/day, outside time/place) and rules that all incur מעילה.
Rabbi Yehoshua states a general rule: anything that had a permitted time for priests (שעת היתר לכהנים) does not incur מעילה, while anything that did not, does.
The mishnah gives examples of offerings that had a permitted time: those that were left overnight (לנה), became impure (נטמאה), or were taken outside (יצאה).

The mishnah gives examples of offerings that never had a permitted time: those slaughtered outside time (חוץ לזמנו), outside place (חוץ למקומו), or whose blood was received and thrown by disqualified priests.

items.text: Gemara's First Question and Answer
items.text_en: Gemara's First Question and Answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah needs to state that slaughtering in the south incurs מעילה, since it seems obvious. It explains that one might have thought that since Ulla said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that dead sacrifices are exempt from מעילה, slaughtering in the south is like choking them. The mishnah teaches that the south, though unfit for קדשי קדשים, is fit for קדשים קלים, so מעילה applies.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: why is this ruling necessary? Is it obvious that slaughtering in the south removes them from מעילה?

The gemara explains it was necessary: one might have thought, based on Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan that dead offerings are exempt from מעילה, that offerings slaughtered in the south are like strangled ones.
The gemara resolves: dead offerings are entirely unfit, but the south, though unfit for קדשי קדשים, is fit for קדשים קלים (lesser holy offerings).

items.text: Why All the Cases?
items.text_en: Why All the Cases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah needs to list all these cases. It explains that each case is necessary: if only the first case were taught, one might think that only when the blood was received in the north does מעילה apply, but not when received in the south. If only the second case were taught, one might think that daytime is the time for offering, but slaughtering at night would exempt. If only the third case were taught, one might think that receiving blood by day incurs מעילה, but slaughtering by day and sprinkling at night would exempt. The mishnah teaches that all these cases incur מעילה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: why does the mishnah need to list all these cases?
The gemara explains: if only the first case were taught, one might think that receiving in the north preserves מעילה, but slaughter in the north and receive in the south would exempt.
The gemara continues: if only the day/night case were taught, one might think that daytime is the time for offering, but slaughter at night would exempt.

The gemara concludes: if only the night/day case were taught, one might think that receiving blood by day preserves מעילה, but slaughter by day and throw at night would exempt; thus all cases are needed.

items.text: The Case of Outside Its Time and Place
items.text_en: The Case of Outside Its Time and Place
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the case of חוץ לזמנו וחוץ למקומו serves, since such an animal is completely invalid. It answers that since it can still effect פיגול, it is not entirely worthless, so מעילה applies.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: what are offerings slaughtered outside time or place fit for?
The gemara answers: because they effect פיגול (pigul — sacrificial invalidation with intent) — they are fit to render the offering pigul.

items.text: The question and initial dispute
items.text_en: The question and initial dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if animals that were disqualified by being slaughtered in the south were brought up on the altar, may they be taken down? Rabbah says they must be taken down; Rav Yosef says they may not be taken down.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if animals disqualified by being slaughtered in the south were brought up on the altar, may they be taken down?
Rabbah rules that if such animals were brought up, they must be taken down.
Rav Yosef rules that if such animals were brought up, they may not be taken down.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute's context
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute's context
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is only according to Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Yehuda, as all agree with Rabbi Yehuda that they must descend.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef applies only according to Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Yehuda, since all agree with Rabbi Yehuda that if they ascended they must descend.

items.text: Rabbah's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbah's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbah argues that Rav Yosef's view aligns with Rabbi Shimon, but Rabbi Shimon's leniency only applies when the blood was received in the proper place; here, since the slaughter was in the south, it is as if they were strangled, so they must descend.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that Rav Yosef's view aligns with Rabbi Shimon, but Rabbi Shimon's leniency only applies when slaughter and blood reception were in the proper place (north); here, since slaughter was in the south, it is as if the animals were strangled, so they must descend.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that one is liable for me'ilah for offerings slaughtered in the south. This challenges Rabbah, who would expect no me'ilah. The Gemara answers that the me'ilah is rabbinic, not Torah-level.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that one is liable for me'ilah (מעילה, misuse of sanctified property) for offerings slaughtered in the south, challenging Rabbah's position that such offerings are invalid and should not incur me'ilah.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the me'ilah mentioned in the Mishnah is only rabbinic (מדרבנן), not Torah-level (דאורייתא).

items.text: Difference between Torah and rabbinic me'ilah
items.text_en: Difference between Torah and rabbinic me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference: Torah-level me'ilah requires payment of the principal plus a fifth, while rabbinic me'ilah does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Torah-level and rabbinic me'ilah.
The Gemara answers that Torah-level me'ilah requires payment of the principal plus a fifth (חומש), while rabbinic me'ilah does not.

items.text: Support from Ulla's statement
items.text_en: Support from Ulla's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is such a thing as rabbinic me'ilah, and proves from Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan that dead offerings have no Torah me'ilah but do have rabbinic me'ilah, supporting the answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is such a thing as rabbinic me'ilah (מעילה).
The Gemara answers yes, citing Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that dead offerings are exempt from Torah me'ilah but have rabbinic me'ilah.
The Gemara concludes that here too the me'ilah is rabbinic.

items.text: Why Ulla's statement was necessary
items.text_en: Why Ulla's statement was necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even though the Mishnah already implies rabbinic me'ilah, Ulla's statement was needed to counter a possible assumption that dead offerings, being completely separated, might not even have rabbinic me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah already teaches Ulla's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara explains that Ulla's statement was necessary to counter a possible assumption that dead offerings, being completely separated, might not even have rabbinic me'ilah.

items.text: Support from a Mishnah on dead offerings
items.text_en: Support from a Mishnah on dead offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about benefiting from a chatat: when alive, one is not liable until causing a loss; when dead, one is liable immediately. This supports the idea of rabbinic me'ilah for dead offerings, though the Gemara notes a possible distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between benefiting from a live chatat (requiring damage for me'ilah) and a dead chatat (immediate liability), supporting the existence of rabbinic me'ilah for dead offerings.
The Gemara begins a brief digression, noting that one might have thought otherwise, but the Mishnah's ruling is conclusive.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that a chatat, which comes for atonement, is not set aside from benefit, but other kodashim are set aside and have no me'ilah. The mishnah teaches that me'ilah does apply to them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that a chatat, which comes for atonement, is not set aside from benefit, but other kodashim are set aside and have no me'ilah; the mishnah teaches that me'ilah does apply to them.

items.text: Objection from a mishnah
items.text_en: Objection from a mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Does a chatat that died have me'ilah? The mishnah states that chatat offerings that died and money sent to the Dead Sea are forbidden for benefit but have no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a chatat that died has me'ilah, citing a baraita that such animals are neither benefited from nor subject to me'ilah.

items.text: Answer: Distinction between living and dead
items.text_en: Answer: Distinction between living and dead
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Chatat offerings that died are set aside from benefit while alive, but the mishnah's case is where it is still alive and not set aside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that chatat offerings that die are set aside from benefit while alive, but the mishnah's case is where the animal is still alive and not set aside.

items.text: Rav Yosef's refutation of Rabbah
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's refutation of Rabbah
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a baraita about sacrifices whose disqualification occurred in the sanctuary, which states that they are not subject to me'ilah. This contradicts Rabbah's position, and the Gemara declares it a conclusive refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rav Yosef challenged Rabbah with a baraita that lists sacrifices that are subject to me'ilah.
The baraita specifies that only the bird sin-offering performed below the red line is exempt from me'ilah, implying all other sacrifices are subject.
The Gemara cites a related baraita about sacrifices disqualified in the sanctuary, which are not subject to me'ilah, contradicting Rabbah's position.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita constitutes a conclusive refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of Rabbah's position.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on a private bamah olah
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on a private bamah olah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef is obvious to Rabbi Elazar, who rules that an olah from a private bamah that was brought into the Temple courtyard is subject to me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef was obvious to Rabbi Elazar, who stated a rule about a private bamah olah brought into the Temple.
Rabbi Elazar rules that an olah (עולה) from a private bamah (במה) that was brought into the Temple courtyard is subject to me'ilah (מעילה).

items.text: Opening statement on partitions
items.text_en: Opening statement on partitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the partitions (walls) of the Temple courtyard absorb (accept) any sanctified item brought inside, implying that once inside, it cannot be removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Temple courtyard partitions absorb any sanctified item brought inside, implying it cannot be removed.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about a disqualified burnt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about a disqualified burnt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether a burnt-offering from a private altar that was brought into the Temple and then disqualified, if it ascended the altar, may descend. The Gemara clarifies the debate between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding whether partitions that are properly constructed (כתיקנה) disqualify, while improperly constructed ones do not. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether a private-altar burnt-offering that was brought into the Temple courtyard and then disqualified, if it ascended the altar, may be taken down.
The Gemara infers that since Rabbi Elazar asks only one case, the other case is already settled for him, either according to Rabbah or Rav Yosef.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's question is actually one case derived from another.

The Gemara elaborates the doubt: perhaps Rabbah's ruling that if it ascended it descends applies only when the partition is properly functioning, but when it is not properly functioning it does not disqualify.

The Gemara raises the alternative doubt: perhaps even according to Rav Yosef, who says if it ascended it does not descend, a properly functioning partition absorbs but an improperly functioning one does not; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement on piggul and me'ilah
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement on piggul and me'ilah
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel reports in the name of Rav that the act of sprinkling blood that renders a sacrifice piggul does not remove the sacrifice from the laws of me'ilah for קדשי קדשים, nor does it bring קדשים קלים into me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that the sprinkling of a piggul (sacrifice rendered invalid by intent) does not remove liability for מעילה (misuse of sanctified property) from קדשי קדשים (most holy things) nor does it bring liability for מעילה in קדשים קלים (lesser holy things).

items.text: Abaye's teaching and Rav Pappa's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's teaching and Rav Pappa's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye teaches Rav Giddel's statement. Rav Pappa objects from a baraita about the todah offering: if slaughtered with piggul intent, the bread becomes sanctified, implying piggul does bring about me'ilah. Abaye is silent.

sub.desc_en: Abaye was sitting and stating this teaching, and Rav Pappa raised an objection from a baraita about one who slaughters a todah (thanksgiving offering) inside the Temple and its bread outside the wall — the bread is not sanctified.

The baraita continues: if he slaughtered it before the bread's faces crusted in the oven, or even if all but one crusted, the bread is not sanctified; but if he slaughtered it outside its time or outside its place, the bread is sanctified.
Rav Pappa concludes that this shows piggul does bring liability for מעילה (misuse), and Abaye was silent.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's resolution: the case involves sprinkling
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's resolution: the case involves sprinkling
items.desc_en: When Abaye came before Rabbi Abba, he explained that Rav Pappa's objection is about the act of sprinkling (זריקה), not slaughter, so it does not contradict Rav's statement.

sub.desc_en: When Abaye came before Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Abba told him that the distinction lies in the sprinkling (זריקה) — the baraita refers to the sprinkling of the blood, not the slaughter.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rava: Ulla said that a piggul handful (קומץ) taken to the altar loses its piggul status, and kemitzah is analogous to slaughter. Rava responds that the prohibition that brings about piggul is different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Rava: Ulla said that a piggul handful (קומץ) brought up to the altar loses its piggul status, and the handful-taking (קמיצה) is analogous to slaughter (שחיטה).
Rava answers that the prohibition that brings about piggul status is what is at issue, not the piggul itself.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's implication
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah already taught that if others bring about piggul, the one who does so himself certainly does. It then clarifies that the issue is about the prohibition of bringing about piggul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the Mishnah already taught that if others bring about piggul, the one who does so himself certainly does — so why is the Mishnah's case needed?
The Gemara answers: here too, the Mishnah is teaching about the prohibition of bringing about piggul (not about the piggul status itself).

items.text: Ravina's challenge from Ilfa's distinction
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge from Ilfa's distinction
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing Ilfa's view that the dispute about combining intentions applies only to two separate services, but in one service all agree it is a mixture of intentions. The Gemara then applies this to the case of sprinkling blood.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing Ilfa's view that the dispute about combining intentions applies only to two separate services.
Ilfa illustrates that in one service, all agree it is a mixture of intentions, unlike two separate services.
The Gemara applies Ilfa's distinction to the case of sprinkling blood, leaving it unresolved whether it is one service or two.

items.text: Gemara's objection regarding the todah offering
items.text_en: Gemara's objection regarding the todah offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if so, regarding the todah offering as well, the status would not be determined until the sprinkling of blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the principle applies to the todah offering as well, the status would not be determined until the sprinkling of blood.

items.text: Clarification of the term 'kadash'
items.text_en: Clarification of the term 'kadash'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the term 'kadash' in the Mishnah means 'becomes disqualified' and requires burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the term 'kadash' in the Mishnah means the meat becomes disqualified (נִפְסָל) and requires burning (שְׂרֵיפָה).

items.text: Supporting evidence and resolution
items.text_en: Supporting evidence and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a supporting baraita that one always commits me'ilah with piggul, but resolves that it refers to a case where the blood was not sprinkled. Alternatively, it refers to an olah offering, where the entire animal is consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that a baraita stating that one always commits me'ilah with piggul supports the previous position, even after the blood was sprinkled.
The Gemara rejects the support by arguing that the baraita refers to a case where the blood was not sprinkled, but then questions the obviousness of such a statement.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita indeed refers to a case where the blood was sprinkled, but it deals with an olah offering, where the entire animal is consecrated to God, so me'ilah applies regardless.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge from the Mishnah's seifa
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge from the Mishnah's seifa
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the seifa of the Mishnah states that if the blood of a sin-offering lingered overnight, one is liable for me'ilah even if the blood was later sprinkled. This supports the view that the Mishnah discusses a sin-offering, not a burnt-offering, because for a burnt-offering it would be obvious that me'ilah applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the seifa of the Mishnah, which states that if the blood of a sin-offering lingered overnight one is liable for me'ilah even after sprinkling, supports the view that the Mishnah discusses a sin-offering, because for a burnt-offering this would be obvious and unnecessary to state.

items.text: Distinction between lingering and improper intention
items.text_en: Distinction between lingering and improper intention
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the seifa indeed supports the view that the Mishnah discusses a sin-offering, but the reisha does not necessarily support it. The reason is that lingering involves a physical action (placing the blood overnight), so sprinkling does not remove me'ilah, whereas improper intention (pigul) involves no physical action, so sprinkling might remove me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the reisha (first clause) of the Mishnah also supports the view that it discusses a sin-offering, given that the seifa (later clause) clearly does.

The Gemara explains that the seifa does not necessarily support the view, because lingering (הלנה) involves a physical action (placing the blood overnight), so sprinkling does not remove me'ilah (מעילה).
The Gemara resolves that improper intention (מחשבה) involves no physical action, so sprinkling does remove me'ilah, distinguishing it from lingering.

items.text: Attempted support from pigul in most holy offerings
items.text_en: Attempted support from pigul in most holy offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether a Mishnah about pigul in most holy offerings supports the view that me'ilah applies even after sprinkling. It initially suggests that the Mishnah implies me'ilah applies even after sprinkling, but then rejects this, arguing that the Mishnah refers to a case where the blood was not sprinkled. The Gemara then notes that if sprinkling did remove me'ilah, the Mishnah should have distinguished between before and after sprinkling in the reisha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that a Mishnah about pigul in most holy offerings supports the view that me'ilah applies even after sprinkling, suggesting it applies even when the blood was sprinkled.
The Gemara rejects the support, arguing that the Mishnah refers to a case where the blood was not sprinkled.
The Gemara objects that if sprinkling removes me'ilah, the Mishnah should have distinguished between before and after sprinkling in the reisha.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's failure to distinguish proves that me'ilah applies even after sprinkling, thus supporting the view.

items.text: Distinction between most holy and lesser holy offerings
items.text_en: Distinction between most holy and lesser holy offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the seifa of the Mishnah about lesser holy offerings is conclusive, but the reisha about most holy offerings is not, because the ruling for lesser holy offerings is absolute (me'ilah does not apply after sprinkling), whereas for most holy offerings it is not absolute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the seifa (lesser holy offerings) is conclusive because the ruling is absolute (no me'ilah after sprinkling), but the reisha (most holy offerings) is not conclusive because the ruling is not absolute.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's principle and its examples
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's principle and its examples
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states a general rule: any offering that had a permitted time for priests is not subject to me'ilah, while one that never had such a permitted time is subject to me'ilah. Examples of the former include offerings that lingered, became impure, or left the courtyard; examples of the latter include offerings slaughtered outside its proper time or place, or whose blood was received or sprinkled by disqualified priests.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states a general rule: any offering that had a permitted time for priests is not subject to me'ilah, while one that never had such a permitted time is subject to me'ilah.
Rabbi Yehoshua lists examples of offerings that had a permitted time for priests: those that lingered, became impure, or left the courtyard.

Rabbi Yehoshua lists examples of offerings that never had a permitted time for priests: those slaughtered outside its proper time or place, or whose blood was received or sprinkled by disqualified priests.

items.text: Bar Kappara's instruction to Bar Pedat
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's instruction to Bar Pedat
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara tells Bar Pedat to ask in the study hall the next day about the phrase 'permission of slaughter' that they learned, implying a question about the application of Rabbi Yehoshua's principle.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara instructs Bar Pedat to ask in the study hall the next day about the phrase 'permission of slaughter' that they learned, implying a question about the application of Rabbi Yehoshua's principle.

items.text: Dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about which 'heter' (permissive act) the Mishnah refers to when it says there is no me'ilah for certain disqualified sacrifices. Chizkiyah says it is the heter of shechitah, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is the heter of achilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's term 'heter' refers to the permissive act of sprinkling (זריקה) or eating (אכילה).
Chizkiyah answers that the Mishnah refers to the permissive act of slaughter (שחיטה).
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah refers to the permissive act of eating (אכילה).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira argues that the Mishnah's language does not support either Chizkiyah or Rabbi Yochanan. He attempts to prove that the Mishnah refers to the heter of zerikah by citing the case of blood that remained overnight, but the Gemara deflects by suggesting the blood was already sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira opens by asserting that the Mishnah's language does not align with either Chizkiyah's or Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation.

Rabbi Zeira cites the Mishnah's case of blood that remained overnight (שלנה) and notes that the Mishnah rules there is no מעילה (misappropriation), implying the blood was already permitted through sprinkling.
Rabbi Zeira infers from the Mishnah that the ruling refers to the heter of sprinkling (היתר זריקה), not eating.

The Gemara rejects Rabbi Zeira's proof by clarifying that the Mishnah's case of 'שלנה' refers to meat that remained overnight, while the blood had already been sprinkled, so the ruling does not support the heter of sprinkling.

items.text: Proof from the case of invalid recipients
items.text_en: Proof from the case of invalid recipients
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Mishnah about a sacrifice that never had a 'time of fitness' for the priests, where invalid recipients received the blood but valid priests sprinkled it. The Mishnah says there is me'ilah, implying that the heter of zerikah is the operative concept.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing cases of a sacrifice that never had a 'time of fitness' for the priests, including invalid recipients who received and sprinkled the blood.
The Gemara asks: if both the recipients and the sprinklers were invalid, why mention both conditions?
The Gemara concludes that the case must be where invalid recipients received the blood but valid priests sprinkled it, and the Mishnah rules that there is me'ilah.
The Gemara infers from this that the Mishnah's rule about me'ilah is based on the concept of היתר זריקה (the permission of sprinkling), not on the permission of eating.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection from the law of kibus
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection from the law of kibus
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges the proof by citing a baraita about a disqualified chatat whose blood does not require kibus. The baraita distinguishes between cases where the sacrifice had a time of fitness and those that never did, and the Gemara concludes that the distinction is not precise, undermining the earlier proof.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges the earlier proof by citing a baraita about a disqualified chatat whose blood does not require kibus, arguing that if the distinction between cases with and without a time of fitness were precise, the baraita would not lump them together.

The baraita defines cases where the sacrifice had a time of fitness (e.g., leftover, impure, or taken out) and those that never had it (e.g., slaughtered outside its place or time, or with invalid reception and sprinkling).

The Gemara asks: if the baraita's case is where both reception and sprinkling were done by invalid priests, then only there is no kibus requirement; but if both were done by valid priests, the blood would require kibus.

The Gemara resolves that the distinction is not precise, citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִזֶּה מִדָּמָהּ' (which sprinkles from its blood) to exclude blood that has already been sprinkled, concluding that the baraita's categories are not exact.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction about me'ilah and shirayim
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction about me'ilah and shirayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the mishnah's mention of me'ilah is not precise, but Rav Asi objects. It then concludes that me'ilah is precise, and the mishnah teaches that a disqualified person can create shirayim, but if a disqualified person received and a qualified person threw, or vice versa, it is meaningless because the blood is shirayim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah's mention of me'ilah is not precise, just as in the earlier case.
Rav Asi objects: if me'ilah is not precise, why does the mishnah need to teach two cases?

The Gemara concludes that me'ilah is precise, and the mishnah teaches that a disqualified person can create shirayim (remnant blood), but if a disqualified person received and a qualified person threw, or vice versa, it is meaningless because the blood is shirayim.

items.text: Resolving Reish Lakish's question about a disqualified person creating shirayim
items.text_en: Resolving Reish Lakish's question about a disqualified person creating shirayim
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan whether a disqualified person can create shirayim. Rabbi Yochanan replied that only piggul (out of time or place) can create shirayim, since it effects atonement for its piggul status. The Gemara clarifies that this includes even a disqualified person, and then reinterprets the statement to mean that only a tamei person (who is accepted in the community) can create shirayim, but other disqualified persons cannot.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether a disqualified person (פָּסוּל) can create shirayim (שִׁירַיִים, leftover sacrificial portions that become permitted for consumption).

Rabbi Yochanan answers that only piggul (פִּגּוּל, sacrifice offered with intent outside its proper time or place) can create shirayim, because piggul effects atonement (מְרַצִּין) for its piggul status.
The Gemara asks: does this imply that a disqualified person is excluded from creating shirayim?
The Gemara answers: no, even a disqualified person can create shirayim.
The Gemara objects: but Rabbi Yochanan said 'אֵין לְךָ' (you have nothing), which implies exclusion.

The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Yochanan's statement: only a person who is not accepted in the community (like piggul) cannot create shirayim, but a tamei person (טָמֵא, who is accepted in the community) can create shirayim; other disqualified persons who are not accepted cannot.

items.text: Examining whether piggul is subject to me'ilah
items.text_en: Examining whether piggul is subject to me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that piggul always has me'ilah, suggesting that the blood was not thrown, implying that the allowance of throwing is what we learned. It then rejects this, saying the blood was thrown, and the word 'always' teaches like Rav Giddel: throwing piggul does not remove from me'ilah nor bring to me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that piggul always has me'ilah, to challenge the previous discussion.
The Gemara infers that the baraita implies the blood was not thrown, suggesting that the allowance of throwing is what we learned.
The Gemara rejects the inference, stating that the blood was indeed thrown.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'always' teaches like Rav Giddel's statement: throwing piggul does not remove from me'ilah nor bring to me'ilah.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's distinction for nosar
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's distinction for nosar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that there is leftover (nosar) that is subject to me'ilah and leftover that is not. The example: if it remained overnight before sprinkling, me'ilah applies; after sprinkling, me'ilah does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Shimon's statement that there is leftover (נוֹתָר) subject to me'ilah and leftover not subject to me'ilah, with the distinction being before or after sprinkling.

items.text: Gemara's inference and rejection regarding heter akhilah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and rejection regarding heter akhilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the case of before sprinkling that there was time to sprinkle, so me'ilah applies, suggesting the rule is based on heter akhilah (permission to eat). It rejects this by positing that the offering was received close to sunset, leaving no time to sprinkle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's ruling that me'ilah applies before sprinkling, implying there was time to sprinkle, so the rule is based on היתר אכילה (permission to eat).
The Gemara explicitly asks whether the mishnah teaches the principle of היתר אכילה (permission to eat).
The Gemara rejects the inference, positing that the offering was received close to sunset, leaving no time to sprinkle.

items.text: Challenge and resolution on the wording 'before sprinkling'
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution on the wording 'before sprinkling'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah says 'before sprinkling' instead of 'before sunset'. It resolves that the mishnah means 'before it becomes fit for sprinkling' (i.e., before the time when sprinkling is possible).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if there was time to sprinkle, would the same ruling apply (i.e., no מעילה)?
The Gemara objects: why does the mishnah say 'before sprinkling' rather than 'before sunset' and 'after sunset'?
The Gemara resolves: the mishnah actually means 'before it becomes fit for sprinkling' and 'after it becomes fit for sprinkling'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's parallel distinction for piggul
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's parallel distinction for piggul
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states a similar rule for piggul: before sprinkling, me'ilah applies; after sprinkling, me'ilah does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita of Rabbi Shimon regarding piggul (פִּיגּוּל), with the same distinction: before sprinkling me'ilah applies, after sprinkling it does not.
Rabbi Shimon explains the distinction: before the sprinkling of the blood, me'ilah applies; after sprinkling, me'ilah does not apply.

items.text: Inference and rejection for piggul
items.text_en: Inference and rejection for piggul
items.desc_en: The Gemara again infers that before sprinkling implies there was time to sprinkle, supporting heter akhilah. It rejects this by saying there was no time to sprinkle, and questions whether having time would exempt from me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that before sprinkling there was time to sprinkle, and therefore the ruling that one is liable for me'ilah (מעילה) supports the principle that היתר אכילה (permission to eat) is the operative factor.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the case involved no time to sprinkle, and then questions whether having time would exempt from me'ilah (מעילה).

items.text: Challenge and resolution on wording for piggul
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution on wording for piggul
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges why the mishnah says 'after sprinkling' instead of 'after sunset', and resolves that it means 'after it becomes fit for sprinkling'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah uses the phrase 'after sprinkling' instead of 'before sunset' and 'after sunset'.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah means 'before it becomes fit for sprinkling' and 'after it becomes fit for sprinkling'.

items.text: Final inference and principle about sprinkling
items.text_en: Final inference and principle about sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about piggul in most holy sacrifices, inferring that sprinkling is the key. It concludes that sprinkling done properly brings into me'ilah, while even improper sprinkling removes from me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that piggul in most holy sacrifices has me'ilah, and infers that this refers to a case where sprinkling was performed, supporting the principle that היתר אכילה (permission to eat) is the criterion.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the baraita refers to a case where sprinkling was not performed, and questions whether after sprinkling there would be no me'ilah.
The Gemara questions why the baraita distinguishes between most holy and lesser holy sacrifices, rather than simply stating the rule in terms of before and after sprinkling.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches a general principle: sprinkling performed לכתחילה (properly) brings into me'ilah, while even improper sprinkling removes from me'ilah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on meat that left before blood sprinkling
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on meat that left before blood sprinkling
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents the case of meat of most holy offerings that left the courtyard before the blood was sprinkled. Rabbi Eliezer rules that one is liable for misuse (me'ilah) but not for piggul, nosar, or tum'ah; Rabbi Akiva rules that there is no misuse but one is liable for those other violations.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of meat of most holy offerings that left the courtyard before blood sprinkling, and presents Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one is liable for misuse (מעילה) but exempt from piggul, nosar, and tum'ah.
Rabbi Akiva rules that there is no misuse (מעילה) but one is liable for piggul, nosar, and tum'ah.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's argument from the lost sin-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's argument from the lost sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues by analogy: if a sin-offering was lost and another substituted, the blood of one atones for the other's meat, exempting it from misuse. Similarly, the blood should exempt its own meat from misuse, even if the meat left before sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva presents a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) argument: just as the blood of a lost sin-offering that was replaced and then found exempts the meat of its fellow from misuse (מעילה), so too it should exempt its own meat.
Rabbi Akiva concludes that if the blood exempts the meat of its fellow from misuse (מעילה), it is logical that it should exempt its own meat.
Rabbi Akiva concludes by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if the blood exempts the meat of its fellow from misuse, it should certainly exempt its own meat.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on lesser holy offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on lesser holy offerings
items.desc_en: The mishnah continues with a parallel case for the sacrificial portions of lesser holy offerings that left before blood sprinkling. Here the positions are reversed: Rabbi Eliezer says no misuse and no liability for piggul, nosar, or tum'ah; Rabbi Akiva says there is misuse and liability.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the case of limbs of lesser holy offerings that left before blood sprinkling, with Rabbi Eliezer ruling no misuse (מעילה) and no liability for piggul, nosar, or tum'ah.
Rabbi Akiva rules that there is misuse (מעילה) and liability for piggul, nosar, and tum'ah.

items.text: Gemara: Why both cases are necessary
items.text_en: Gemara: Why both cases are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah needs to teach both cases (most holy and lesser holy). It explains that if only most holy were taught, one might think Rabbi Eliezer's leniency applies only there; if only lesser holy, one might think Rabbi Akiva's stringency applies only there. Both are needed to clarify the full scope of their dispute.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the mishnah needs to state both cases (most holy and lesser holy offerings).

The gemara explains that both cases are necessary: without the first, one might think Rabbi Eliezer's leniency applies only to most holy offerings, and without the second, one might think Rabbi Akiva's stringency applies only to lesser holy offerings.

The Gemara explains that if only lesser holy were taught, one might think Rabbi Akiva's stringency applies only there, but Rabbi Eliezer's leniency would also apply to most holy; therefore both cases are needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's limitation and Rav Asi's report
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's limitation and Rav Asi's report
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Akiva's ruling that blood sprinkling affects meat that left applies only to meat that partially left, not entirely. Rav Asi then reports that his colleagues in the diaspora taught him something (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that Rabbi Akiva's ruling that sprinkling affects misuse (מעילה) applies only to meat that partially left the courtyard, not to meat that entirely left.
Rabbi Assi tells Rabbi Yochanan that his colleagues in the diaspora have already taught him this principle.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one can have improper intent (מחשבה) regarding an item that is lost or burned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one can have improper intent (מחשבה) regarding an item that is lost or burned.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Asi's inquiry
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Asi's inquiry
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how intent can apply to something that no longer exists, citing Rav Asi's question to Rabbi Yochanan about intent for spilled blood. Rabbi Zeira responds that just as a 'lul' (a type of vessel) without substance does not receive impurity, so too spilled blood is unaffected by intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can the Mishnah speak of intent for lost or burnt items that no longer exist in the world?

sub.text: Rav Asi's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Asi's inquiry to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Asi's question to Rabbi Yochanan: what is the law if one had intent for blood that will be spilled tomorrow?
Rabbi Zeira answers by analogy to a 'lul' (a vessel without substance) that cannot receive impurity, so too spilled blood, destined for loss, is unaffected by intent.

items.text: Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah refers to items destined to be lost or burned, not those already lost or burned.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the Mishnah's phrase 'עַל הָאָבוּד וְעַל הַשָּׂרוּף' (on the lost and the burned) as referring to items destined to be lost or burned (עַל הָעוֹמֵד לְאִיבּוּד וְעַל הָעוֹמֵד לִישָּׂרֵף), not items already lost or burned.

items.text: Rav Papa's statement on Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Rav Papa's statement on Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: Rav Papa clarifies that Rabbi Akiva's principle that sprinkling effects atonement for blood that has left the sanctuary applies only when the meat left, but not when the blood itself left.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa resolves that Rabbi Akiva's principle of sprinkling effecting atonement for blood that left the sanctuary applies only when the meat left, but not when the blood itself left.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Papa: if one slaughtered silently and blood exited, even if he later sprinkled it, it is ineffective; for most holy sacrifices there is מעילה, for lesser holy ones there is not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Papa's position: if one slaughtered silently and blood exited, even if he later sprinkled it, it is ineffective; for most holy sacrifices there is מעילה (misappropriation), for lesser holy ones there is not.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva compares the case to a lost sin-offering, and Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies only when both animals are slaughtered simultaneously, not sequentially.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks a rhetorical question: 'To what is this case comparable?'
Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies only when both animals are slaughtered simultaneously (בבת אחת), not sequentially (בזה אחר זה).

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's testimony and Rabbi Akiva's proof
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's testimony and Rabbi Akiva's proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon recounts his encounter with an elder and the Galilean sages who questioned Rabbi Akiva's view. Rabbi Akiva then proves his position from the case of a lost sin-offering: if one set aside a replacement and later found the original, both are subject to מעילה, and their blood in cups also has מעילה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon recounts that an elder asked him whether Rabbi Akiva holds that sprinkling effects atonement for blood that has exited, and the Galilean sages objected that a disqualified offering cannot effect atonement.

Rabbi Akiva proves his position from the case of a lost sin-offering: if one set aside a replacement and later found the original, both are subject to מעילה (misappropriation), and their blood in cups also has מעילה.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's argument to the student
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's argument to the student
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues that if the blood of one sin-offering exempts its own meat from me'ilah, it should also exempt the meat of its fellow, even if the fellow is invalid. He then argues that if it exempts the fellow's meat, it should certainly exempt its own meat.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's question to the student
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's question to the student
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks the student to concede that if the blood of one sin-offering exempts its own meat from me'ilah, it should also exempt the meat of its fellow.
Rabbi Akiva argues that if the blood exempts the fellow's meat even though it is invalid, it should certainly exempt its own meat.

items.text: Resh Lakish's objection in the name of Rav Oshaya
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's objection in the name of Rav Oshaya
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish, citing Rav Oshaya, calls Rabbi Akiva's response a 'stolen answer' (תשובה גנובה), arguing that the case of simultaneous offerings (בבת אחת) differs from sequential ones (בזה אחר זה). He questions why there should be any difference since both are invalid.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish, citing Rav Oshaya, objects that Rabbi Akiva's answer is a 'stolen answer' (תשובה גנובה), because it only works for simultaneous offerings (בבת אחת) but not for sequential ones (בזה אחר זה).
Resh Lakish asks rhetorically why there should be any difference between simultaneous and sequential offerings, since both are invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument and Resh Lakish's silence
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument and Resh Lakish's silence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish with a case of two guilt-offerings set aside as replacements, where one's sacrificial portions were offered before blood sprinkling. He argues that if they were considered one entity, the portions would not descend from the altar, contradicting Ulla's principle. Resh Lakish is silenced, and Rabbi Yochanan declares he 'cut off the legs of the child' (i.e., defeated the young scholar).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Resh Lakish whether he agrees with the principle that blood of one offering exempts its fellow from מעילה (misuse).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument with a case of two guilt-offerings
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument with a case of two guilt-offerings
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that if two guilt-offerings were set aside as replacements and one's sacrificial portions were offered before blood sprinkling, they would descend from the altar, contradicting Ulla's principle that קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) portions offered before blood sprinkling do not descend.

sub.text: Resh Lakish's silence and Rabbi Yochanan's declaration
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish's silence and Rabbi Yochanan's declaration
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish is silenced, and Rabbi Yochanan declares he 'cut off the legs of the child' (i.e., defeated the young scholar).

items.text: Mishnah: The effect of blood sprinkling on me'ilah
items.text_en: Mishnah: The effect of blood sprinkling on me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood sprinkling has both lenient and stringent effects on Most Holy Things, but only stringent effects on Lesser Holy Things. It details the rules of me'ilah before and after sprinkling for both categories, and notes that piggul, notar, and tum'ah apply in all cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that blood sprinkling has both lenient and stringent effects on Most Holy Things, and details the rules of me'ilah before and after sprinkling for that category.
The Mishnah adds that piggul, notar, and tum'ah apply to both the meat and the sacrificial portions of Most Holy Things after sprinkling.
The Mishnah states that for Lesser Holy Things, blood sprinkling has only stringent effects, and details the rules of me'ilah before and after sprinkling for that category.
The Mishnah concludes that piggul, notar, and tum'ah apply to both the meat and the sacrificial portions of Lesser Holy Things after sprinkling.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'no me'ilah' regarding meat after sprinkling, implying there is still an issur (prohibition). It asks why there should be any prohibition since the meat is the priest's property. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrasing is merely stylistic, using 'no me'ilah' in contrast to 'me'ilah' in the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's phrase 'אין מועלין בבשר' (no me'ilah in the meat) implies that there is still an issur (prohibition), asking why there should be any prohibition since the meat is the priest's property.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrasing is merely stylistic, using 'אין מועלין' in contrast to 'מועלין' in the first clause, and does not imply a real prohibition.

items.text: Gemara's question on Lesser Holy Things
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Lesser Holy Things
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the same question regarding Lesser Holy Things: why does the Mishnah say 'no me'ilah' for meat after sprinkling, implying an issur, when the meat belongs to the owners?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the same question regarding Lesser Holy Things: why does the Mishnah say 'no me'ilah' for meat after sprinkling, implying an issur, when the meat belongs to the owners?

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's answer: It refers to meat that left the courtyard
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's answer: It refers to meat that left the courtyard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that the Mishnah refers to meat that has left the Temple courtyard (ליוצאין), and follows Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling is effective only for meat that is fit for burning (ליוצא לשריפה).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that the Mishnah refers to meat that has left the Temple courtyard (ליוצאין), and follows Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling is effective only for meat that is fit for burning (ליוצא לשריפה).

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter by stating that the offering is not acceptable for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the offering is not acceptable for eating.

items.text: Return to chapter
items.text_en: Return to chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the return to the current chapter with the phrase 'Haderan alach'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the return to the current chapter with the phrase 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that for a bird sin-offering, meilah applies from the moment of consecration. Once its neck is pinched, it becomes susceptible to disqualification by immersion of a tevul yom, lack of atonement, or overnight stay. After its blood is sprinkled, one is liable for piggul, notar, and tumah, but there is no meilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that for a bird sin-offering, meilah applies from the moment of consecration.
Once its neck is pinched, it becomes susceptible to disqualification by immersion of a טבול יום (one who immersed that day), lack of atonement, or overnight stay.
After its blood is sprinkled, one is liable for piggul, notar, and tumah, but there is no meilah.

items.text: Gemara's question on susceptibility
items.text_en: Gemara's question on susceptibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says the offering becomes susceptible to disqualification (l'hipasel) but not to impart impurity (l'tamuyei). It asks which authority holds this view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Mishnah states the offering becomes susceptible to disqualification (לִיפָּסֵל) but not to impart impurity (לְטַמּוֹיֵי), and asks which authority holds this view.

items.text: Gemara's answer: Abba Shaul
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: Abba Shaul
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, as it is taught in a baraita that Abba Shaul says a tevul yom can disqualify but not impart impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, not Abba Shaul.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Abba Shaul states that a tevul yom (one who immersed that day) can disqualify but not impart impurity.

items.text: Mishnah: Tevul Yom and Kodashim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Tevul Yom and Kodashim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a tevul yom is considered 'beginning to be sacred' (תחילה לקדש). Rabbi Meir says he renders kodashim impure and terumah invalid, while the Sages say he invalidates both terumah and kodashim equally.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a tevul yom is considered 'beginning to be sacred' (תחילה לקדש).
Rabbi Meir states that a tevul yom renders kodashim impure (מטמא) and invalidates terumah (פוסל).
The Sages argue that a tevul yom invalidates both terumah and kodashim equally, without distinction between impurity and invalidation.

items.text: Gemara: Rava Explains the Dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava Explains the Dispute
items.desc_en: Rava explains that according to Abba Shaul, the Sages made a special stringency for kodashim, treating a tevul yom like a first-degree impurity. For Rabbi Meir, he is like a second-degree food; for the Sages, since he immersed, his impurity is weakened—he can invalidate but not render impure.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by explaining that according to Abba Shaul, the Sages made a special stringency (מעלה) for kodashim, treating a tevul yom (one who immersed that day) as a first-degree impurity (ראשון).

Rava continues by distinguishing the positions: for Rabbi Meir, the tevul yom is like a second-degree food (אוכל שני); for the Sages, since he immersed, his impurity is weakened—he can invalidate (פוסל) but not render impure (טמא).

items.text: Question: Why is There Me'ilah for Bird Sin-Offering Blood?
items.text_en: Question: Why is There Me'ilah for Bird Sin-Offering Blood?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The Mishnah says that if one sprinkled the blood of a bird sin-offering, one is liable for me'ilah. But why? The blood belongs to the priests! Rabbi Chanina answers: This refers to a bird that went out (became disqualified), and it follows Rabbi Akiva who holds that sprinkling is effective for a disqualified bird, since it is not fit for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The Mishnah says one is liable for me'ilah when sprinkling the blood of a bird sin-offering, but why? The blood belongs to the priests!
Rabbi Chanina answers: The Mishnah refers to a disqualified bird that went out, and follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that sprinkling is effective for such a bird because it is not fit for eating.

items.text: Dispute: Is the Squeezing of the Blood Essential?
items.text_en: Dispute: Is the Squeezing of the Blood Essential?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav says that the squeezing (מיצוי) of the bird sin-offering's blood does not impede the atonement, as Rav taught the verse 'he sprinkled its blood'. Rav Adda bar Ahavah citing Rav says it does impede, as Rav taught 'he squeezed its blood'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav states that the squeezing (מיצוי) of the bird sin-offering's blood does not impede atonement, citing Rav's teaching of the verse 'he sprinkled its blood'.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah citing Rav contradicts, asserting that the squeezing does impede atonement, citing Rav's teaching of the verse 'he squeezed its blood'.

items.text: Proof from the Verse
items.text_en: Proof from the Verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a verse: 'And the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out... it is a sin-offering.' This supports Rav Adda bar Ahavah. For Rav Huna, the word 'remainder' is explained by the school of Rabbi Yishmael as meaning 'if some remained', and 'it is a sin-offering' refers to the first sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a verse to support Rav Adda bar Ahavah, and then questions how Rav Huna would interpret the word 'remainder'.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that 'remainder' means 'if some remained', and 'it is a sin-offering' refers to the first sprinkling, resolving Rav Huna's difficulty.

items.text: Rav Acha's Objection from the Meal-Offering
items.text_en: Rav Acha's Objection from the Meal-Offering
items.desc_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava asks Rav Ashi: If so, regarding the meal-offering where it is written 'and the remainder', would we also say 'if it remained'? The Gemara begins to consider this objection.

sub.text: Rav Acha the son of Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava objects to Rav Ashi: If the principle applies, then regarding the meal-offering where it is written 'וְהַנּוֹתֶרֶת' (and the remainder), would we also interpret it as 'if it remained'?

items.text: Resolution of contradiction regarding missing ingredients
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction regarding missing ingredients
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that excludes a meal-offering missing flour, oil, or frankincense, but resolves it by noting the extra word "והנותרת" in the verse, indicating a special case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that excludes a meal-offering missing flour, oil, or frankincense.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting the extra word "והנותרת" in the verse, indicating a special case.

items.text: Challenge and resolution about bird-offering blood squeezing
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution about bird-offering blood squeezing
items.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel challenges Rav Huna with a baraita that mentions squeezing blood of bird-offerings, implying it is essential. Rav Huna himself resolves that the baraita is stated in a divided manner, referring to different cases.

sub.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel challenges Rav Huna by citing a baraita that explicitly mentions squeezing blood (מיצה דמן) for bird-offerings, implying it is an essential act.
Rav Huna himself resolves the challenge by explaining that the baraita is stated in a divided manner (לצדדין), referring to different cases.

items.text: Dispute about whether remaining blood is essential
items.text_en: Dispute about whether remaining blood is essential
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael who says that if blood remains (after squeezing), it is valid, implying squeezing is not essential. Rav Pappa notes a dispute between two Tannaim regarding the requirement of squeezing for a bird sin-offering.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael states that if blood remains after squeezing, the offering is valid, implying squeezing is not essential.
The Gemara notes a contradiction: another teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael states that the remnants (שיריים) are essential, implying squeezing is required.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that the dispute between the two Tannaim concerns specifically the requirement of squeezing (מיצוי) for a bird sin-offering.
The Gemara concludes that the two positions represent a dispute between two Tannaim, both aligned with Rabbi Yishmael's school.

items.text: Mishnah: Stages of me'ilah for various offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stages of me'ilah for various offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the stages at which me'ilah applies to different offerings: from consecration until disposal of ashes, with intermediate stages for disqualification and liability for piggul, notar, and tum'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the stages of me'ilah for the bird burnt-offering (עולת העוף), from consecration until disposal of ashes.
The Mishnah lists the stages of me'ilah for the burnt bulls and goats (פרים הנשרפים ושעירים הנשרפים), from consecration until the flesh melts in the ash-pit.
The Mishnah lists the stages of me'ilah for the animal burnt-offering (עולה), from consecration until disposal of ashes, noting that me'ilah does not apply to the hides.
The Mishnah lists the stages of me'ilah for sin-offering, guilt-offering, and communal peace-offerings (חטאת, אשם, זבחי שלמי ציבור), from consecration until disposal of the sacrificial portions.
The Mishnah lists the stages of me'ilah for the two loaves (שתי הלחם), from consecration until the blood of the lambs is sprinkled, after which me'ilah ceases.
The Mishnah lists the stages of me'ilah for the showbread (לחם הפנים), from consecration until the bowls of frankincense are offered, after which me'ilah ceases.

The Mishnah concludes by listing the stages of me'ilah for meal-offerings (מנחות), from consecration until the handful is taken, after which me'ilah applies only to the handful until disposal of ashes.

items.text: Debate about me'ilah on ashes from the altar
items.text_en: Debate about me'ilah on ashes from the altar
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether one is liable for me'ilah on ashes from the altar's apple (pile of ashes). Both agree before the removal of ashes there is liability; they disagree after removal. Rav says no, as the mitzvah is fulfilled; Rabbi Yochanan says yes, because the ashes still require priestly garments. The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah and resolves it by Rav's interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan regarding me'ilah on ashes from the altar's apple (pile of ashes).
The Gemara clarifies that both agree there is liability before the removal of ashes, and the dispute is only after removal.
Rav argues that after removal, there is no liability because the mitzvah of removing the ashes has been fulfilled.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that liability continues because the ashes still require priestly garments for their removal, so they retain sanctity.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah, which states that liability continues until the ashes leave for the ash-pit, challenging Rav's position.
Rav resolves the contradiction by interpreting the Mishnah's phrase 'עַד שֶׁתֵּצֵא לְבֵית הַדֶּשֶׁן' as meaning 'until it is designated for the ash-pit,' not until it actually leaves.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about coals falling from the altar
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about coals falling from the altar
items.desc_en: A baraita states that coals that fell from the altar are not returned. This appears to contradict Rav's view that ash has no substance, so the Gemara answers that coals have substance while ash does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that coals that fell from the altar are not returned, which challenges Rav's view that ash has no substance.
Rav answers that coals have substance (משָׁשָׁא), unlike ash, so the baraita does not contradict his view.

items.text: Alternative version: dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Alternative version: dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: An alternative version reverses the problem: the baraita's ruling is due to coals having substance, so ash without substance would not be subject to me'ilah even on the altar. This challenges Rabbi Yochanan, who defends by saying the rule is the same for ash, and the baraita specifically mentions coals to teach that even coals are not returned.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reverses the objection: the baraita's ruling about coals challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view that ash has substance, not Rav's.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the same rule applies even to ash, and the baraita mentions coals only to teach that even coals with substance are not returned.

Rabbi Yochanan responds that the same rule applies even to ash, and the baraita specifically mentions coals to teach that even coals, which have substance, are not returned once they fall from the altar.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Levi on the penalty for benefit from sacrificial meat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Levi on the penalty for benefit from sacrificial meat
items.desc_en: Rav and Levi argue about one who benefits from meat of קדשי קדשים before blood application or from אימורי קדשים קלים after blood application: Rav says the value falls to נְדָבָה; Levi says the person must bring an item entirely consumed on the altar.

sub.desc_en: A dispute is stated: Rav and Levi disagree about the disposition of benefit from sacred meat before blood is thrown.
Rav rules that the value of the benefit falls to נְדָבָה (a freewill offering).
Levi rules that the person must bring an item entirely consumed on the altar.

items.text: Baraita supporting Levi
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Levi
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that one who benefits from such sacrificial meat must bring an item entirely consumed on the altar, namely incense.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Levi: the students say one brings an item entirely for the altar, identified as incense (קטורת).

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav and a general rule
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav and a general rule
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who benefits from blood of a sin-offering or guilt-offering before atonement must add and bring more of the same, but once the offering has been sacrificed, the value goes to the Dead Sea or falls to נְדָבָה. A general rule follows: offerings for the altar go to the altar, etc.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav: one who benefits from sin-offering or guilt-offering blood before atonement adds and brings the offering, but after atonement the money goes to the Dead Sea or falls to a donation.
The baraita adds a general rule: offerings for the altar go to the altar, Temple maintenance offerings go to maintenance, and communal offerings go to communal נְדָבָה (free-will offerings).

items.text: Contradiction in the baraita resolved by Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Contradiction in the baraita resolved by Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The baraita seems internally contradictory: before atonement, one adds the same offering; after atonement, the money goes to the Dead Sea. Yet it also says all altar offerings go to the altar. The Gemara resolves that the first clause follows Rabbi Shimon, who says a sin-offering whose owners have atoned must die.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause says that after the sin-offering has been brought the money goes to the Dead Sea, but the baraita also states that all altar offerings go to the altar, regardless of atonement.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first clause to Rabbi Shimon, who rules that a sin-offering whose owners have already atoned must die (תמות).

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Geviha from Bei Katil reports in the name of Abaye that the first clause of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon and the latter clause follows the Rabbis, thereby resolving the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's first clause can follow Rabbi Shimon and the latter clause follow the Rabbis, given the apparent contradiction.

sub.text: Rav Geviha from Bei Katil in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Geviha from Bei Katil in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Geviha from Bei Katil reports in the name of Abaye that the first clause follows Rabbi Shimon and the latter clause follows the Rabbis, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Rava's ruling on benefiting from impure sanctified meat
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on benefiting from impure sanctified meat
items.desc_en: Rava states that all agree one is exempt from me'ilah if they benefit from meat of Kodshei Kodashim that became impure before the blood was thrown, or from limbs of Kodashim Kalim after they were offered up. The Gemara questions why this is necessary to state, and explains that it teaches that the mitzvah of burning or turning them over does not create liability.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that all agree one is exempt from me'ilah when benefiting from impure meat of Kodshei Kodashim before the blood is thrown, or from limbs of Kodashim Kalim after they are offered up.
The Gemara asks why Rava's ruling is necessary, since the benefit causes no loss to sanctity.
The Gemara explains that Rava's ruling is needed to teach that the mitzvah to burn the impure meat or turn the limbs over does not create liability for me'ilah.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding the law of 'already a sin-offering has been offered'
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding the law of 'already a sin-offering has been offered'
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the principle that money for a sin-offering whose owner has died goes to the Dead Sea applies only when the death was known before atonement, but after atonement the money falls to a free-will offering, because one does not initially designate something for destruction.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes that the rule that money for a sin-offering whose owner died goes to the Dead Sea applies only when the death was known before atonement, but after atonement the money falls to a free-will offering, because one does not initially designate something for destruction.

items.text: Mishnah: Items subject to me'ilah from sanctification and the general rule
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items subject to me'ilah from sanctification and the general rule
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items such as the handful, frankincense, incense, and various meal-offerings that are subject to me'ilah from the moment of sanctification. Once sanctified in a vessel, they become susceptible to disqualification by a tevul yom, one lacking atonement, or being left overnight, and one is liable for notar and tum'ah but not piggul. The general rule is that anything with permiters is not liable for piggul, notar, or tum'ah until the permiters are offered, while anything without permiters is liable for notar and tum'ah once sanctified in a vessel, but not piggul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items subject to me'ilah from the moment of sanctification.

The Mishnah states that once sanctified in a vessel, these items become susceptible to disqualification by a tevul yom, one lacking atonement, or being left overnight, and one is liable for notar and tum'ah but not piggul.
The Mishnah gives the general rule: anything with permiters is not liable for piggul, notar, or tum'ah until the permiters are offered.
The Mishnah states the converse rule: anything without permiters is liable for notar and tum'ah once sanctified in a vessel, but not piggul.

items.text: Gemara's derivation from a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation from a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that liability for impurity applies only to offerings with permiters. It proposes a kal vachomer from piggul: just as piggul, which is less severe, applies only to offerings with permiters, so too impurity, which is more severe, should apply only to such offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that liability for impurity applies only to offerings with permiters.

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from piggul to impurity, arguing that since piggul, which is less severe, applies only to offerings with permiters, impurity, which is more severe, should likewise apply only to such offerings.

items.text: Scriptural derivation and limitation
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation and limitation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer and cites a verse to include all sacred items, but then limits liability to the time of approach (when permiters are brought).

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites a verse to teach that the impurity law applies to all sacred items, but the phrase 'who approaches' indicates that liability is not immediate.
The Gemara limits liability to the time of approach (when permiters are brought), citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִקְרַב' (who approaches).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar clarifies the rule: for offerings with permiters, liability begins when the permiters are brought; for offerings without permiters, liability begins when they are sanctified in a vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar resolves the apparent contradiction: one is liable for impurity only after the permiters are offered for offerings with permiters, or after sanctification in a vessel for offerings without permiters.

items.text: Conclusion of chapter and Mishnah listing sin-offerings that die
items.text_en: Conclusion of chapter and Mishnah listing sin-offerings that die
items.desc_en: The daf concludes the chapter on bird sin-offerings and presents the Mishnah listing cases where a sin-offering animal must die: offspring of a sin-offering, its substitute, a sin-offering whose owners died, one that passed its year, and one that was lost and found blemished after atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter on bird sin-offerings with the formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).
The Mishnah lists the first three cases where a sin-offering must die: its offspring, its substitute, and one whose owners died.
The Mishnah adds two more cases: a sin-offering that passed its year, and one that was lost and found blemished after atonement — these die and have no benefit or מעילה (misuse of sacred property).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the first clause (where the Sages do not dispute) and the second clause (where they do). The answer is that the first clause is an explicit ruling, while the second is not explicit. The Gemara then notes that the ruling about temurah was taught elsewhere, but here it is taught in the context of meilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's first clause has no dispute while the second clause has a dispute.
The Gemara answers that the first clause is an explicit ruling, while the second is not explicit, so the Sages dispute it.
The Gemara objects that the ruling about temurah was already taught elsewhere, so why repeat it here?
The Gemara resolves that the ruling is taught here because of the context of meilah (misuse of sacred property), not because of temurah.

items.text: Mishnah: Money set aside for nezirut
items.text_en: Mishnah: Money set aside for nezirut
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that money designated for a nazirite's offerings may not be benefited from nor is there meilah, because it is suitable for shelamim. If the nazirite dies, unspecified money goes to a freewill offering; specified money for a chatat goes to the Dead Sea, for an olah brings an olah with meilah, and for shelamim brings shelamim eaten in one day without bread.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that money set aside for a nazirite's offerings may not be benefited from and is not subject to מעילה (misuse of sacred property), because all of it is suitable for shelamim offerings.
The Mishnah rules that if the nazirite dies, unspecified money goes to a freewill offering.
The Mishnah rules that specified money for a chatat goes to the Dead Sea and is neither benefited from nor subject to מעילה.
The Mishnah rules that specified money for an olah brings an olah and is subject to מעילה.
The Mishnah rules that specified money for shelamim brings shelamim, eaten in one day and not requiring bread.

items.text: Resh Lakish's challenge and Rava's response
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's challenge and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish challenges the Mishnah, asking why it does not also teach the case of money set aside for bird offerings (kinim), which would also be prohibited from benefit and meilah because they are suitable for turtledoves not yet in season or pigeons past their season. Rava responds that the Torah says to bring shelamim with unspecified money, but does it say to bring turtledoves not in season? They are not fit for the altar.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish challenges the Mishnah, asking why it does not also teach the case of money set aside for bird offerings (kinim), which would also be prohibited from benefit and meilah because they are suitable for turtledoves not yet in season or pigeons past their season.
Rava responds that the Torah says to bring shelamim with unspecified money, but does it say to bring turtledoves not in season? They are not fit for the altar.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon on blood and libations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon on blood and libations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon says: Blood is lenient at the beginning and stringent at the end; libations are stringent at the beginning and lenient at the end.
