Initially, there is no meilah in blood; after it is poured into the Kidron brook, there is meilah. For libations, initially there is meilah; after they go into the shittin (underground channels), there is no meilah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states the general principle: blood is lenient at the beginning and stringent at the end, while libations are stringent at the beginning and lenient at the end.

Rabbi Shimon elaborates: initially there is no מעילה (misappropriation) in blood, but after it flows to the Kidron brook there is; for libations, initially there is מעילה, but after they descend to the שיתין (underground channels) there is none.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over meilah in blood
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over meilah in blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon say there is meilah in blood; the Sages say there is none. Ulla explains the Sages' view from the verse 'And I have given it to you' – it is yours. The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: 'to atone' – I gave it for atonement, not for meilah. Rabbi Yochanan derives from 'for the blood atones through the soul' that before atonement is like after atonement: just as after atonement there is no meilah, so before atonement there is none. The Gemara objects: perhaps the opposite – before atonement there is meilah, and after atonement as well? The Gemara counters: Is there any item whose mitzvah has been performed and yet meilah applies? Why not?

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon hold that there is meilah in blood, while the Sages hold there is none.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Sages who say there is no meilah in blood.
Ulla derives from the verse 'And I have given it to you' that the blood is yours, implying no meilah.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the blood was given for atonement (כפרה), not for meilah.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse that before atonement is like after atonement: just as after atonement there is no meilah, so before atonement there is none.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the opposite inference — before atonement there is meilah, and after atonement as well.
The Gemara rejects the objection: is there any item whose mitzvah has been performed and yet meilah applies? Why not? (implying that after atonement, meilah cannot apply).

items.text: Question on terumat hadeshen and me'ilah
items.text_en: Question on terumat hadeshen and me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why terumat hadeshen, which has fulfilled its mitzvah, still has me'ilah. It answers that this is because terumat hadeshen and the limbs of the scapegoat are two verses that come as one, and such verses do not teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why terumat hadeshen (the ash removal), which has fulfilled its mitzvah, still has me'ilah (misappropriation liability).
The Gemara answers that terumat hadeshen and the limbs of the scapegoat are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד), and such verses do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Alternative answer for those who permit benefit from scapegoat limbs
items.text_en: Alternative answer for those who permit benefit from scapegoat limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works only for those who say one may not benefit from the scapegoat's limbs. For those who permit benefit, it offers another answer: terumat hadeshen and the priestly garments are two verses that come as one, so they do not teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works only for those who say one may not benefit from the scapegoat's limbs, and asks what can be said for those who permit benefit.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: terumat hadeshen and the priestly garments are two verses that come as one, so they do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Dosa's view
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Dosa's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works for the Rabbis who say the garments require burial, but for Rabbi Dosa who permits a common priest to use them, a different answer is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works for the Rabbis who require burial of the garments, but for Rabbi Dosa who permits a common priest to use them, a different answer is needed.

items.text: Answer using the heifer whose neck is broken
items.text_en: Answer using the heifer whose neck is broken
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that terumat hadeshen and the heifer whose neck is broken (eglah arufah) are two verses that come as one, so they do not teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that terumat hadeshen and the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה) are two verses that come as one, so they do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Refutation for those who say such verses do teach
items.text_en: Refutation for those who say such verses do teach
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that this works only for those who say two verses do not teach a principle. For those who say they do, it explains that there are two exclusions: 'the heifer' and 'and he shall place it beside the altar', indicating that only these items are excluded, not others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this works for those who say two verses do not teach a principle, but for those who say they do teach, what can be said?
The Gemara answers: two exclusions are written — 'the heifer' and 'and he shall place it beside the altar' — indicating that only these items are excluded, not others.

items.text: Discussion on nesakhim and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's view
items.text_en: Discussion on nesakhim and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the mishnah's ruling that nesakhim have me'ilah at the start aligns with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, who describes a pit where wine residue is burned in sanctity. Ravina derives this from a verbal analogy between 'kodesh' here and in the case of notar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's ruling that nesakhim have me'ilah at the start contradicts Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's view.
A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok describing a small pit where wine residue is burned in sanctity, derived from the verse 'בַּקֹּדֶשׁ הַסֵּךְ נֶסֶךְ שֵׁכָר לַה׳'.
The Gemara asks what the scriptural derivation is for this practice.

Ravina derives the law via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'קֹדֶשׁ' used in the verse about notar, teaching that just as notar is burned in sanctity, so too the wine residue is burned in sanctity.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah could even align with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, if the wine was absorbed (קלט) into the pit before me'ilah applies.

An alternative version suggests the mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, but the Gemara rejects this, arguing that the verse is merely an אסמכתא (supportive allusion) and the actual law is rabbinic.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: mishnah as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: mishnah as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
items.desc_en: Some say the mishnah aligns with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok if the wine was absorbed. Others reject this, saying the mishnah is rabbinic and the verse is merely a support (asmakhta).

sub.desc_en: Some propose that the mishnah can still align with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok if the wine was absorbed (קְלַט) into the ground before being burned.
An alternative version asks whether the mishnah actually follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, specifically when the wine was absorbed.
Others answer that the mishnah is not from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok but is a rabbinic enactment.
The gemara objects: but the mishnah cites a verse as its source, so how can it be merely rabbinic?
The gemara resolves that the verse is merely an אסמכתא (a scriptural support, not a binding derivation), so the mishnah remains rabbinic.

items.text: Mishnah on ashes of inner altar and menorah
items.text_en: Mishnah on ashes of inner altar and menorah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one may not benefit from the ashes of the inner altar and menorah, nor is there me'ilah. If one consecrates such ashes initially, me'ilah applies. Similarly, doves that are too young and pigeons that are too old are forbidden for benefit but have no me'ilah. The Gemara begins to analyze this.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that the ashes of the inner altar and menorah are forbidden for benefit but entail no me'ilah, with an exception for consecrating ashes initially, and similarly for doves and pigeons out of their proper age.
The Gemara begins its analysis by introducing a question about the mishnah.

items.text: Source for placing ashes of inner altar and menorah
items.text_en: Source for placing ashes of inner altar and menorah
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the biblical source for placing ashes of the inner altar, deriving it from a verse about the outer altar through a verbal analogy. It then extends the source to include the menorah by a double usage of the word 'deshen'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the source for placing ashes of the outer altar is explicit in the verse, but from where do we derive the same for the inner altar?
Rabbi Elazar derives the inner altar from a verbal analogy: the verse about removing the crop applies to the inner altar if not needed for the outer altar.
The Gemara objects: perhaps both clauses refer to the outer altar, one to establish its location.
The Gemara resolves: if only the outer altar were intended, the verse would not have used the extra word 'הדשן' (the ash), which extends to the inner altar.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the source for the menorah, and answers by noting the double usage of the word 'דשן' (ash) in the verse.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon on birds offered before or after their time
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon on birds offered before or after their time
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that according to Rabbi Shimon, turtledoves that have not reached their proper time are subject to me'ilah, but pigeons that have passed their proper time may not be benefited from nor are they subject to me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Shimon's ruling: turtledoves that have not reached their proper time are subject to me'ilah, but pigeons that have passed their proper time may not be benefited from nor are they subject to me'ilah.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that an animal offered before its time is subject to a negative commandment but not karet. It then questions why the Rabbis distinguish this case from a blemished animal, and answers that birds have no redemption because a blemish does not disqualify them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon's position is consistent with his stated reasoning: an animal offered before its time is subject to a negative commandment but not karet.
The Gemara asks why the Rabbis distinguish this case from a blemished animal (מחוסר זמן), which has redemption.
The Rabbis answer that a blemished animal is subject to redemption, but birds have no redemption because a blemish does not disqualify them.

items.text: Ulla's statement on me'ilah for consecrated animals that died
items.text_en: Ulla's statement on me'ilah for consecrated animals that died
items.desc_en: Ulla quotes Rabbi Yochanan that consecrated animals that died are exempt from me'ilah by Torah law. Rav Chisda objects, citing the Mishnah's case of birds that are not subject to me'ilah despite their sanctity. Ulla concedes there is rabbinic me'ilah, and the Gemara resolves the objection by comparing to blood, which initially has no me'ilah but later does.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that consecrated animals that died are exempt from me'ilah by Torah law.
Rav Chisda objects, questioning where the sanctity of the animals went if they are exempt from me'ilah.
Ulla responds by citing the Mishnah about birds that are not subject to me'ilah, implying the same question applies there.
Ulla concedes that there is rabbinic me'ilah for consecrated animals that died, but questions how something can initially lack me'ilah and later acquire it.
The Gemara cites the case of blood, which initially has no me'ilah but later acquires it when poured into the Kidron brook, as a precedent.
The Gemara resolves the objection by noting that even in the blood case, there is me'ilah from the outset (rabbinically), so the parallel holds.

items.text: Rav's ruling on blood from a consecrated animal
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on blood from a consecrated animal
items.desc_en: Rav states that blood drawn from a consecrated animal is forbidden for benefit and one is liable for me'ilah. Rav Hamnuna challenges this from the Mishnah that says fat and eggs of consecrated animals are not subject to me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that blood drawn from a consecrated animal is forbidden for benefit and one is liable for me'ilah.
Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav from the Mishnah that fat and eggs of consecrated animals are not subject to me'ilah.

items.text: Answer: Blood is essential, fat is not
items.text_en: Answer: Blood is essential, fat is not
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that blood is essential for the animal's survival, so it is considered part of the consecrated body, whereas fat is not essential, so it is not subject to me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that blood is essential for the animal's survival, so it is considered part of the consecrated body, whereas fat is not essential, so it is not subject to me'ilah.

items.text: Challenge from manure and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from manure and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges from a baraita that manure in the Temple courtyard is not subject to me'ilah, even though it is not essential. The Gemara resolves that manure comes from outside the animal, whereas blood comes from the animal's own body.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges from a baraita that manure and dung in the Temple courtyard are not subject to me'ilah and their proceeds go to the chamber, implying that even non-essential items are exempt.
The Gemara questions why manure is exempt, since the animal can survive without it, just like the blood case.
The Gemara answers that manure comes from external food consumed by the animal, whereas blood comes from the animal's own body, so the distinction stands.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Elazar's principle
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Elazar's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's ruling that the proceeds of such items go to the Temple treasury supports Rabbi Elazar's principle: wherever the Sages say something is 'sacred but not sacred,' its proceeds go to the treasury.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's ruling that the proceeds of such items go to the Temple treasury supports Rabbi Elazar's principle: wherever the Sages say something is 'sacred but not sacred,' its proceeds go to the treasury.

items.text: Mishnah: Fat and eggs of consecrated animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Fat and eggs of consecrated animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that fat and eggs of consecrated animals are not subject to me'ilah. This applies to animals consecrated for the altar, but for animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, one may be liable for me'ilah on the animal and its products.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the fat and eggs of consecrated animals are neither benefited from nor subject to me'ilah.
The Mishnah distinguishes: for animals consecrated for the altar, the rule applies; for animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, one may be liable for me'ilah on the animal and its products.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between altar and maintenance consecration. Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: the ruling applies only when the animal is consecrated with inherent sanctity for the altar, but if consecrated with monetary sanctity for the altar, it is treated like maintenance consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: if an animal is consecrated with monetary sanctity (קדושת דמים) for the altar, why does the Mishnah say there is no מעילה (misuse) in its milk or eggs?

Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: the ruling applies only when the animal is consecrated with inherent sanctity (קדושת הגוף) for the altar, but if consecrated with monetary sanctity (קדושת דמים) for the altar, it is treated like maintenance consecration (בדק הבית), so one does commit מעילה in its milk or eggs.

items.text: Mishnah: Consecrating a container with its contents
items.text_en: Mishnah: Consecrating a container with its contents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between consecrating a container (like a pit, ash-heap, dovecote, tree, or field) that already contains something, in which case both the container and its contents are subject to meilah, versus consecrating the container first and then it later fills, in which case only the container is subject to meilah, not the contents.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if one consecrates an item for both the Temple maintenance and the altar, one may commit meilah (misuse of consecrated property) with it, and then asks 'How so?' to introduce the examples.

The Mishnah lists examples of consecrating a container that is already full: a pit full of water, an ash-heap full of dung, a dovecote full of pigeons, a tree full of fruit, and a field full of grass.
The Mishnah rules that when consecrating a container that is already full, one may commit meilah (misuse of consecrated property) both with the container and with its contents.

The Mishnah shifts to the contrasting case: if one consecrates the container first and it later fills, one may commit meilah (misuse of consecrated property) only with the container, not with the contents.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's opinion on consecrated field and tree
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's opinion on consecrated field and tree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei adds that one who consecrates a field or a tree is liable for meilah on the produce that grows from them, because they are growths of consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that one who consecrates a field or a tree is liable for meilah on their growths, because they are growths of consecrated property.

items.text: Mishnah: Offspring of consecrated animals and workers' restrictions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Offspring of consecrated animals and workers' restrictions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the offspring of a consecrated animal (ma'aser or muqdashin) may not nurse from its mother, but others may donate to feed it. Additionally, workers may not eat from consecrated figs, and similarly a cow may not eat from consecrated vetch.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the offspring of a ma'aser animal may not nurse from its mother, but others may donate to feed it.
The Mishnah rules that the offspring of a muqdashin animal may not nurse from its mother, but others may donate to feed it.
The Mishnah states that workers may not eat from consecrated figs, and similarly a cow may not eat from consecrated vetch.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the law of offspring of ma'aser
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the law of offspring of ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law that the offspring of a consecrated animal (ma'aser) may not nurse from its mother. Rav Achadvoi bar Ami derives it via a verbal analogy (gezerah shavah) of 'ha'avarah' from the firstborn, and similarly for muqdashin via 'imo' from the firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that the offspring of a ma'aser animal may not nurse from its mother, and asks for the scriptural source.

Rav Achadvoi bar Ami derives the law for ma'aser via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'העברה' from the firstborn, establishing that the milk of a ma'aser animal is subject to מעילה (misappropriation).
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami similarly derives the law for muqdashin (other consecrated animals) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'אמו' from the firstborn.

items.text: Gemara: Reason workers may not eat consecrated produce
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason workers may not eat consecrated produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason workers may not eat from consecrated produce: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami cites the verse 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it threshes,' and the word 'dīsho' (its threshing) implies your threshing, not consecrated threshing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason workers may not eat from consecrated produce.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami answers by citing the verse 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it threshes,' interpreting 'דִּישׁוֹ' (its threshing) to mean your threshing, not consecrated threshing.

items.text: Gemara: Threshing attached produce in a consecrated field
items.text_en: Gemara: Threshing attached produce in a consecrated field
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one threshes 'kal'ilin' (a type of plant) in a consecrated field, and Ravina deduces that even the 'abkah' (dust) of the plant causes meilah, implying that the law applies even to attached produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who threshes 'kal'ilin' (a type of plant) in a consecrated field has committed meilah (misuse of consecrated property).
The Gemara objects that meilah normally requires detached produce, but here the 'kal'ilin' are still attached to the ground.
Ravina answers that this case teaches that even the 'abkah' (dust or minute particles) of the plant, which are detached during threshing, cause meilah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Roots, spring, water, and willow
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Roots, spring, water, and willow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that tree roots of an unconsecrated tree that grow into consecrated ground, or vice versa, are not subject to meilah. Similarly, a spring flowing from a consecrated field is not subject to meilah outside the field. Water in a golden flask is not subject to meilah, but once transferred to a glass vessel, it is. The willow branch used in the Temple is not subject to meilah, though Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok notes that elders would use it for their lulavim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that tree roots crossing between unconsecrated and consecrated land are not subject to meilah.
The Mishnah rules that a spring flowing from a consecrated field is not subject to meilah inside the field, but once outside it is permitted.
The Mishnah states that water in a golden flask is not subject to meilah, but once transferred to a glass vessel it is.
The Tanna Kamma rules that the willow branch used in the Temple is not subject to meilah.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok adds that elders would use the willow branch for their lulavim, implying benefit was permitted.

items.text: Resh Lakish's statement on water measure
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's statement on water measure
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish comments that there is no meilah for all the water in the flask, but there is meilah for three log of water, implying a minimum measure.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that there is no me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property) for all the water in the flask, but there is me'ilah for three log of water, implying a minimum measure.

items.text: Gemara's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: The Mishnah's latter clause says 'if he placed them in a glass vessel, one is liable for meilah,' implying that the first clause (water in the flask) has no meilah even for three log, contradicting Resh Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's latter clause implies the first clause has no meilah even for three log, contradicting Resh Lakish.

items.text: Resolution: Resh Lakish's statement applied to the latter clause
items.text_en: Resolution: Resh Lakish's statement applied to the latter clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Resh Lakish's statement was actually said regarding the latter clause: 'One is liable for meilah' – but only for three log.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Resh Lakish's statement was actually said regarding the latter clause: 'One is liable for meilah' – but only for three log.

items.text: Debate between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on water measure
items.text_en: Debate between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on water measure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that meilah applies to all the water, not just three log. The Gemara questions whether Resh Lakish holds that water has a minimum measure, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says one who pours water of the Festival outside is liable, and Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Elazar's view in line with Rabbi Akiva. Resh Lakish then deduces that just as wine for libation is three log, so too water is three log, implying he holds there is no minimum measure for water – but this is only according to Menachem Yodafah's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that meilah applies to all the water in the golden pitcher, not just three log.
The Gemara questions whether Resh Lakish holds that water has a minimum measure (שיעור) for meilah.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that one who pours the water of the Festival libation outside the Temple is liable, implying a minimum measure.
Rabbi Yochanan explains, in the name of Menachem Yodafah, that Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Akiva's method of deriving both water and wine libations from the verse 'נִסְכֵּיהֶם' (their libations).
Resh Lakish deduces that just as wine for libation is three log, so too water is three log, implying he holds there is no minimum measure for water.
The Gemara resolves that Resh Lakish's statement was only according to Menachem Yodafah's reasoning, not his own view.

items.text: Mishnah: Bird nest and grove
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bird nest and grove
items.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes: A bird's nest atop a consecrated tree is not subject to meilah; if atop an asherah (idolatrous tree), one knocks it off with a pole. One who consecrates a thicket is liable for meilah for all of it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a bird's nest atop a consecrated tree is neither benefited from nor subject to meilah.
The Mishnah rules that if the nest is atop an asherah (idolatrous tree), one knocks it off with a pole.
The Mishnah rules that one who consecrates a thicket is liable for meilah for all of it.

items.text: Dispute on an idol that broke on its own
items.text_en: Dispute on an idol that broke on its own
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue about an idol that broke on its own. Rabbi Yochanan forbids it because no gentile nullified it, while Reish Lakish permits it reasoning that if the idol cannot save itself, it cannot save him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan forbids an idol that broke on its own, while Reish Lakish permits it.
The gemara explains each position: Rabbi Yochanan forbids because no gentile nullified it; Reish Lakish permits because the idol's inability to save itself implies it cannot save the worshipper.

items.text: Reish Lakish's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita about a bird's nest on an asherah, where one knocks it off with a pole, implying the asherah is permitted. Rabbi Yochanan deflects by saying the nest was made from wood brought from elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing a baraita about a bird's nest on an asherah, where one knocks it off with a pole, implying the asherah itself is permitted.
Rabbi Yochanan deflects by explaining that the nest was made from wood brought from elsewhere, not from the asherah itself.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita distinguishes between consecrated wood and asherah if the wood is from elsewhere, and resolves that the case involves later growths, and one holds that there is no me'ilah in growths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the baraita refers to wood brought from elsewhere, why does it distinguish between consecrated wood (where one may not benefit and there is no me'ilah) and asherah wood (where one knocks the nest off with a stick)?

The Gemara resolves: the case involves later growths (גידולין) of the tree, and the Tanna holds that there is no me'ilah in growths, so the consecrated tree's growths are permitted, while the asherah's growths are forbidden and must be knocked off.

items.text: Support and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Support and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports the resolution by arguing that if the wood were from elsewhere, one could simply take the nest. Rabbi Avahu then quotes Rabbi Yochanan reinterpreting 'knocks' as referring to knocking off the chicks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the previous resolution by arguing that if the wood were from elsewhere, one could simply take the nest rather than knock it off.
Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan reinterpreting 'knocks' as referring to knocking off the chicks, not the nest itself.

items.text: Distinction between chicks and eggs
items.text_en: Distinction between chicks and eggs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov tells Rabbi Yirmeya that chicks are permitted in both cases, but eggs are forbidden. Rav Ashi adds that if chicks need their mother, they are like eggs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov tells Rabbi Yirmeya that chicks are permitted in both cases (asheirah and hekdesh), but eggs are forbidden in both.
Rav Ashi adds that if chicks need their mother, they are like eggs (i.e., forbidden).

items.text: Mishnah on treasurers purchasing wood
items.text_en: Mishnah on treasurers purchasing wood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that treasurers who purchase wood incur me'ilah for the wood but not for the shavings or chips.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that treasurers who purchase wood incur me'ilah for the wood itself but not for the shavings or chips.

items.text: Shmuel's statement on building and consecrating
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement on building and consecrating
items.desc_en: Shmuel says one builds with mortar and then consecrates, because a donor consecrates money onto the building by saying 'let the sanctity of the money take effect on the building,' and then gives it to the craftsmen as their wages.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that one builds with mortar and then consecrates the building.
The Gemara explains that a donor consecrates money by saying 'let the sanctity of the money take effect on the building.'
The donor then gives the consecrated building to the craftsmen as their wages.

items.text: Baraita on leftover ketoret
items.text_en: Baraita on leftover ketoret
items.desc_en: The baraita describes what was done with leftover ketoret funds: they were used to pay artisans, then redeemed and returned to new terumah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the procedure for leftover ketoret funds: they were used to pay artisans, redeemed against their wages, given to them, and then taken back from new terumah.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the funds aren't used for building, and answers that there is no building project at that time, or insufficient funds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the leftover incense funds are not redeemed for building (בנין) instead of paying workers.
The Gemara answers that there is no building project at that time.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly mentions 'workers' funds' (מעות האומנין), implying a building project exists.
The Gemara refines the answer: there is no building project requiring a sum equal to the available funds.

items.text: Objection from Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Objection from Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects based on Shmuel's ruling that even a small amount can redeem a large consecrated item, but concludes that this is only post-facto, not initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Shmuel's ruling that a consecrated item worth a maneh can be redeemed post-facto even for a perutah.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's ruling applies only בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation for building in non-sacred area
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation for building in non-sacred area
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that building with sacred funds in the Temple is prohibited because one might inadvertently benefit from the sacred space, so they build in non-sacred areas.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that building with sacred funds in the Temple is prohibited because one might inadvertently benefit from the sacred space, so they build in non-sacred areas.

items.text: Mishnah on wood and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Mishnah on wood and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that treasurers who purchase wood are liable for מעילה, but not for chips or bark. The Gemara questions why they don't buy wood from non-sacred funds, and answers the same concern about potential misuse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that treasurers who purchase wood with sacred funds are liable for מעילה (misuse of sanctified property), but not for the chips or bark.
The Gemara questions why the treasurers do not purchase the wood from non-sacred (חול) funds to avoid the issue of מעילה.
The Gemara answers that if they used non-sacred funds, they might later lie down on the wood, thereby inadvertently misusing sanctified property.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction for wood
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction for wood
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that the Mishnah refers to wood for that day's use, not future wood, which would be handled differently.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the objection by distinguishing between wood for future use (דְּמִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ), which would indeed be handled differently, and the Mishnah's case of wood for that day's use (דְּיוֹמֵיהּ), which is subject to מעילה (misappropriation).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that kodshei mizbe'ach combine with each other for me'ilah and for liability for piggul, nosar, and tamei. Kodshei bedek habayit combine with each other, and both categories combine with each other for me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that kodshei mizbe'ach combine with each other for me'ilah and for liability for piggul, nosar, and tamei, and kodshei bedek habayit combine with each other, and both categories combine with each other for me'ilah.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah separates kodshei mizbe'ach from kodshei bedek habayit, since it already states they combine. It answers that the separation is necessary because the liability for piggul, nosar, and tamei applies only to kodshei mizbe'ach, not to kodshei bedek habayit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the Mishnah already states that kodshei mizbe'ach and kodshei bedek habayit combine with each other, why does it need to separately state that kodshei mizbe'ach combine with each other?
The Gemara answers: because the Mishnah teaches liability for piggul, nosar, and tamei on kodshei mizbe'ach, which does not apply to kodshei bedek habayit, it therefore separates the two categories.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's statement on the scope of me'ilah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's statement on the scope of me'ilah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai asserts that biblical me'ilah applies only to kodshei bedek habayit and burnt offerings (olah), because the verse 'nefesh ki tim'ol ma'al mikadshei Hashem' refers to items exclusively dedicated to God, whereas kodshei mizbe'ach have portions for priests and owners.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that me'ilah applies by Torah law only to kodshei bedek habayit and the olah, because they are entirely dedicated to God, whereas other kodshei mizbe'ach have portions for priests and owners.

Rabbi Yannai explains his reasoning by citing the verse 'נפש כי תמעל מעל מקדשי ה (if a person commits a trespass against the Lord's sacred items)', which he interprets as referring to items exclusively dedicated to God.
Rabbi Yannai concludes that kodshei mizbe'ach are excluded from biblical me'ilah because they have portions for priests and owners, not being exclusively dedicated to God.

items.text: Challenges to Rabbi Yannai from the Mishnah and baraitot
items.text_en: Challenges to Rabbi Yannai from the Mishnah and baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yannai by citing the Mishnah that kodshei mizbe'ach combine for me'ilah, and baraitot that imply me'ilah applies to kodshei kodashim slaughtered in the south and to a chatat after death. The Gemara deflects each by saying these are rabbinic enactments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yannai by citing the Mishnah that kodshei mizbe'ach (sacrifices of the altar) combine with each other for me'ilah (misuse of sacred property).
The Gemara deflects the challenge by stating that the Mishnah's rule is only a rabbinic enactment (מדרבנן), not Torah law.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yannai by citing a baraita that me'ilah applies to kodshei kodashim (most holy sacrifices) slaughtered in the south.
The Gemara deflects this challenge as well, stating that the baraita is only a rabbinic enactment.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yannai by citing the Mishnah that one who benefits from a chatat (sin-offering) after it dies is liable for me'ilah immediately.
The Gemara deflects this challenge as well, stating that the Mishnah's rule is only a rabbinic enactment.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi's baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi's baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a baraita of Rabbi expounds 'kol chelev laHashem' to include emurim of kodashim kalim for me'ilah, implying a biblical source. The Gemara responds that this is merely an asmakhta (scriptural support), not a true derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is there no Torah source? A baraita cites Rabbi who derives me'ilah for emurei kodashim kalim from the verse 'כל חלב לה׳', and answers that this is merely an אסמכתא (supportive allusion).
The Gemara responds that this is merely an asmakhta (scriptural support), not a true biblical derivation.

items.text: Ulla's statement and clarification from Rabbi Yannai's school
items.text_en: Ulla's statement and clarification from Rabbi Yannai's school
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ulla quoting Rabbi Yochanan that sacrifices that died are exempt from biblical me'ilah. It questions whether this refers to kodshei bedek habayit (where even a garbage heap dedicated would still have me'ilah) or kodshei mizbe'ach (which lacks biblical me'ilah). The school of Rabbi Yannai clarifies that the verse teaches about kodshei bedek habayit, not kodshei mizbe'ach.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Ulla quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Ulla quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that sacrifices that died are exempt from biblical me'ilah.
The Gemara asks whether Ulla's statement refers to kodshei bedek habayit (where even a dedicated garbage heap would still have me'ilah) or kodshei mizbe'ach.
The Gemara objects that kodshei mizbe'ach have no biblical me'ilah, so the exemption would be trivial.
The school of Rabbi Yannai clarifies that the verse teaches about kodshei bedek habayit, not kodshei mizbe'ach.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Items that combine for the olah and todah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Items that combine for the olah and todah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that five items combine for the olah (meat, fat, fine flour, wine, oil) and six for the todah (adding bread). This sets the halakhic framework for combination of sacrificial components.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five items that combine for the olah and the six items that combine for the todah.

items.text: Gemara's correction of Rav Huna's misquotation
items.text_en: Gemara's correction of Rav Huna's misquotation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna misquotes the Mishnah as 'five things in the world combine', and Rava corrects him, noting the text says 'in the olah'. Rav Huna then acknowledges the error.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna recites the Mishnah to Rava but mistakenly says 'בָּעוֹלָם' (in the world) instead of 'בָּעוֹלָה' (in the olah).
Rava objects that Rav Huna said 'בָּעוֹלָם' and notes that the Mishnah's todah list includes bread.
Rav Huna accepts the correction and instructs to recite 'בָּעוֹלָה' (in the olah).

items.text: Baraita: Olot and eimurim combine for a k'zayit
items.text_en: Baraita: Olot and eimurim combine for a k'zayit
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that olot and eimurim (sacrificial portions) combine to a k'zayit for liability for offering outside, piggul, notar, and tum'ah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that olot and emurim combine to an olive's bulk for liability of offering outside, piggul, notar, and tum'ah.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why only olah and not shelamim?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why only olah and not shelamim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies olah but not shelamim. For offering outside, olah is wholly burnt, so combination makes sense; but for piggul, notar, and tum'ah, shelamim should also combine, as a Mishnah says all piggulim and notarot combine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies only עולה (burnt offering) and not שלמים (peace offering) for combination regarding piggul, notar, and tum'ah.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that states all piggulim and notarot combine with each other, implying shelamim should also combine.

items.text: Revised interpretation: Olah and its eimurim combine for blood sprinkling
items.text_en: Revised interpretation: Olah and its eimurim combine for blood sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: olah and its eimurim combine to a k'zayit for the purpose of sprinkling blood. Once they combine for that, liability for piggul etc. follows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita: the olah and its eimurim combine to a k'zayit for the purpose of blood sprinkling, and once they combine for that, liability for piggul etc. follows.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Yehoshua and discussion of minchah
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Yehoshua and discussion of minchah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the baraita as Rabbi Yehoshua's view: for all sacrifices, a k'zayit of meat and fat allows blood sprinkling; for olah, even half-k'zayit each suffices; for minchah, even if fully intact, no sprinkling. Rav Pappa explains minchah refers to the minchah of libations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the baraita and identifies it as Rabbi Yehoshua's view.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua's rule: for all sacrifices, a k'zayit of meat and fat allows blood sprinkling; half-k'zayit each does not.
The baraita adds: for עולה (burnt offering), even half-k'zayit each suffices because it is entirely consumed; for מנחה (meal offering), even if fully intact, no sprinkling.
The Gemara asks what מנחה (meal offering) has to do with blood sprinkling, since it has no blood.
Rav Pappa explains that the מנחה (meal offering) referred to is the מנחת נסכים (meal offering of libations) brought with animal sacrifices, which does have blood associated with it.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Terumot combine for prohibition and fifth
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Terumot combine for prohibition and fifth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists terumah, terumat ma'aser, terumat ma'aser of demai, challah, and bikurim as combining to prohibit and obligate the additional fifth. The Gemara explains they all share the name 'terumah', citing verses for challah and bikurim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists terumah, terumat ma'aser, terumat ma'aser of demai, challah, and bikurim as combining to prohibit and obligate the additional fifth.
The Gemara asks why these five items combine.
The Gemara answers that they all share the name 'terumah', citing the verse for challah.
A baraita is cited to show that bikurim are also called 'terumah' from the verse 'וּתְרוּמַת יָדֶךָ', and the Gemara notes that the other items need no proof.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Neveilot and shekatzim combine
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Neveilot and shekatzim combine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all neveilot (carcasses) combine with each other, and all shekatzim (creeping things) combine. The Gemara begins with 'Rav said', but the text cuts off.

items.text: Dispute between Levi and Rav Asi on combination for eating
items.text_en: Dispute between Levi and Rav Asi on combination for eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the earlier ruling about combination applies only to impurity, but for eating, pure and impure items are separate. Levi argues they do combine even for eating, while Rav Asi holds they remain separate. There is a debate about whether Rav Asi disagrees with Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the earlier ruling about combination applies only to impurity, but for eating, pure and impure items remain separate.
Levi argues that pure and impure items do combine even for eating.
Rav Asi holds that pure and impure items remain separate for eating.

sub.text: Stam's report of a dispute about Rav Asi's relation to Rav
sub.text_en: Stam's report of a dispute about Rav Asi's relation to Rav
sub.desc_en: Some say Rav Asi disagrees with Rav, while others say he does not.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Asi from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Asi from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the death of a cow and the life of a camel do not combine, implying that the death of both does combine. This challenges Rav Asi's view that pure and impure items do not combine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Asi by citing a baraita that implies the death of both a cow and a camel combine, contradicting his view that pure and impure items do not combine.

items.text: First answer: Reinterpret the baraita
items.text_en: First answer: Reinterpret the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita actually means the life of both combine, and it follows Rabbi Yehuda who holds that the prohibition of a limb from a living animal applies to impure animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the baraita to mean that the lives of both animals combine, and attributes this view to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the prohibition of a limb from a living animal (אבר מן החי) applies even to impure animals.

items.text: Objection to the first answer
items.text_en: Objection to the first answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the baraita means the life of both, then why mention the death of a cow and the life of a camel? Even the death of both would not combine, making the specific case unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the baraita means the life of both, then why mention the death of a cow and the life of a camel? Even the death of both would not combine, making the specific case unnecessary.

items.text: Second challenge and conclusion
items.text_en: Second challenge and conclusion
items.desc_en: Another baraita is brought that explicitly states that half an olive from a cow and half from a camel, whether alive or dead, combine. This contradicts the first baraita, but the Gemara concludes that the death of both indeed combines, challenging Rav Asi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita that explicitly states that half an olive from a cow and half from a camel, whether alive or dead, combine, contradicting Rav Asi's position.

Rav Asi resolves the contradiction by asserting that this Tanna holds the principle of איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition can take effect upon an existing prohibition), allowing the combination even in death.

items.text: Rav Asi's response
items.text_en: Rav Asi's response
items.desc_en: Rav Asi explains that the tanna of the baraita holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition, allowing combination even for impure items.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi explains that the tanna of the baraita holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition (איסור חל על איסור), allowing combination even for impure items.

items.text: Rav's ruling on eating sheratzim
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on eating sheratzim
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah says in Rav's name that one is liable for eating sheratzim only if he eats a kezayit, because the Torah uses the term 'achilah' (eating) regarding them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah reports in Rav's name that eating sheratzim incurs liability only for a kezayit, because the Torah uses the term 'אכילה' (eating) regarding them.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina taught a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan that a verse begins with eating and ends with impurity, implying that just as impurity is with a k'adayishah, so too eating is with a k'adayishah. Rabbi Yochanan praised this, and this contradicts Rav.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina taught a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan citing the verse that begins with eating and ends with impurity.
The baraita infers that just as impurity applies with a lentil-sized portion (כעדשה), so too eating applies with a lentil-sized portion.
Rabbi Yochanan praised the baraita, and the gemara notes that this contradicts Rav's position.

items.text: Resolution: alive vs. dead
items.text_en: Resolution: alive vs. dead
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the creatures are alive (where the measure is a k'adayishah) and when they are dead (where the measure is a kezayit).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the creatures are dead (the measure is a kezayit) and when they are alive (the measure is a k'adayishah).

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rav Yosef's response
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rav Yosef's response
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rav was basing his ruling on a mishnah that deals with dead sheratzim, so the resolution does not apply. Rav Yosef responds that Rav was merely stating a tradition, not deriving from the mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rav's ruling is based on a mishnah that includes dead sheratzim, so the distinction between live and dead cannot resolve the contradiction.
Rav Yosef responds that Rav was merely stating a tradition (שמעתא בעלמא), not deriving his ruling from the mishnah.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on limbs
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on limbs
items.desc_en: A baraita states that limbs have no minimum measure and can be less than a kezayit or k'adayishah, yet Rabbi Yochanan says one is only liable for a kezayit. This challenges the earlier resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that limbs have no minimum measure and can be less than a kezayit or k'adayishah, yet still convey impurity.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself rules that one is only liable for a kezayit, contradicting the baraita's implication that liability could apply to smaller amounts.

items.text: Rava's answer: distinct creatures
items.text_en: Rava's answer: distinct creatures
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the verse speaks of creatures that are distinct (muvdalim), meaning those that are recognizable as a separate species, not limbs.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the verse speaks of creatures that are distinct (muvdalim), meaning those that are recognizable as a separate species, not limbs.

items.text: Rav Ada bar Ahava's question
items.text_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava's question
items.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava asks Rava: if so, should we also distinguish between a distinct animal and a non-distinct one regarding liability?

sub.text: Rav Ada bar Ahava's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava asks Rava: if Rava's distinction applies to creeping things, should we also distinguish between a distinct animal and a non-distinct one regarding liability?

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Torah's comparison of creeping creatures to other impure things applies only to the prohibition of eating them, not to the measures of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Torah's comparison of creeping creatures to other impure things applies only to the prohibition of eating them (בל תשקצו), not to the measures of impurity.

items.text: Mishnah: Combining blood and flesh of creeping creatures
items.text_en: Mishnah: Combining blood and flesh of creeping creatures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood and flesh of a creeping creature combine for impurity. Rabbi Yehoshua's principle: items with equal impurity and measure combine; if either differs, they do not combine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood and flesh of a creeping creature combine for impurity, and Rabbi Yehoshua's rule: items with equal impurity and measure combine; otherwise they do not.
Rabbi Yehoshua states a general rule: items with equal impurity and measure combine; if either differs, they do not combine.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Chanin quoting Rav Zeira, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina, derive from the plural 'the impure ones' that creeping creatures combine, even blood with flesh, whether from one species or two.

sub.text: Rav Chanin citing Rav Zeira and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Chanin citing Rav Zeira and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanin in the name of Rav Zeira and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina derive from the verse 'הטמאים' that creeping creatures' blood and flesh combine, even different species or different names.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's addition
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's addition
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina adds that the verse extends combination to include even blood with flesh, whether from one or two species.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Entire vs. partial
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Entire vs. partial
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves a contradiction: one source deals with the entire creature, the other with part. He proves this from a baraita about a creeping creature's blood on the floor: if it overshadows part of the floor, it is pure; if the entire floor, it is impure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case dealing with the entire creature (כולו) and one dealing with part of it (מקצתו).
A baraita is cited as proof: blood of a creeping creature spilled on a floor that overshadows part of the floor is pure, but if it overshadows the entire floor, it is impure.
The gemara objects: if 'part' refers to part of the blood, that contradicts Rabbi Chanina's ruling that a quarter-log of blood that stirred in a vessel is pure.
The gemara concludes that the baraita must be understood as distinguishing between the entire floor and part of the floor, confirming Rav Yosef's resolution.

items.text: Rabbi Matya ben Charash's question
items.text_en: Rabbi Matya ben Charash's question
items.desc_en: Rabbi Matya ben Charash asks Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in Rome: from where is it derived that the blood of creeping creatures is impure? Rabbi Shimon answers from the verse 'And this is to you the impure'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Matya ben Charash asks Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai for the source that blood of creeping creatures is impure, and Rabbi Shimon answers from the verse 'וזה לכם הטמא'.
Rabbi Shimon answers from the verse 'וְזֶה לָכֶם הַטָּמֵא' (And this is to you the impure).

items.text: Narrative: Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobli repeals decrees
items.text_en: Narrative: Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobli repeals decrees
items.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon to explain further. He praises Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's wisdom, recounting how Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobli used clever arguments to persuade Roman authorities to repeal decrees against Shabbat, circumcision, and marital purity, though they later recognized him and reinstated them.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai to explain further, and he praises Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's wisdom.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon's narrative about Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobli
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's narrative about Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobli
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon recounts that the Roman government decreed against Shabbat, circumcision, and marital purity.

sub.text: Rabbi Reuven's first argument to the Romans
sub.text_en: Rabbi Reuven's first argument to the Romans
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Reuven argues that an enemy should be impoverished, so they should not work on Shabbat; the Romans agree and repeal the decree against Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbi Reuven's second argument to the Romans
sub.text_en: Rabbi Reuven's second argument to the Romans
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Reuven argues that an enemy should be weakened, so they should circumcise their sons on the eighth day; the Romans agree and repeal the decree against circumcision.

sub.text: Rabbi Reuven's third argument to the Romans
sub.text_en: Rabbi Reuven's third argument to the Romans
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Reuven argues that an enemy should be diminished, so they should not engage in marital relations during menstruation; the Romans agree and repeal the decree against marital purity.
The Romans recognize Rabbi Reuven as a Jew and reinstate the decrees, then ask who will go and repeal them.

items.text: Debate over who should go to Rome
items.text_en: Debate over who should go to Rome
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon argue about sending their sons to Rome to annul decrees, each claiming the other's father would not agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai should go to Rome because he is experienced with miracles, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi should accompany him.
Rabbi Yosi objects that if his father Rabbi Chalafta were alive, they could not ask him to send his son to danger.
Rabbi Shimon counters that if his father Yochai were alive, they could not ask him to send his son to danger either.

items.text: Rabbi Yosi's fear and Rabbi Shimon's punishment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosi's fear and Rabbi Shimon's punishment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi agrees to go but fears Rabbi Shimon's anger; Rabbi Shimon promises not to punish him but does so anyway.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi agrees to go but expresses fear that Rabbi Shimon will punish him.
Rabbi Shimon accepts upon himself not to punish Rabbi Yosi.
Despite the promise, Rabbi Shimon punishes Rabbi Yosi anyway.

items.text: Question on blood of a creeping thing and Rabbi Elazar's response
items.text_en: Question on blood of a creeping thing and Rabbi Elazar's response
items.desc_en: While traveling, a question arises about the impurity of blood of a creeping thing; Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi answers, and Rabbi Shimon recognizes his wisdom, telling him not to return to his father.

sub.desc_en: A question is asked before the group: from where do we know that the blood of a creeping thing (שרץ) is impure?

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi twists his mouth and answers by citing the verse 'וְזֶה לָכֶם הַטָּמֵא' (and this shall be impure to you), implying the blood is included.
Rabbi Shimon recognizes Rabbi Elazar's wisdom from his clever wording and declares that the son should not return to his father.

items.text: Encounter with Ben Temalion and entry to Rome
items.text_en: Encounter with Ben Temalion and entry to Rome
items.desc_en: Ben Temalion offers to accompany them; Rabbi Shimon reflects on the merit of a maidservant. They enter the palace, exorcise Ben Temalion, and are allowed to take whatever they want from the treasury, where they find and tear up a decree.

sub.desc_en: Ben Temalion offers to accompany them; Rabbi Shimon weeps, reflecting on the merit of a maidservant who received angelic visits, and accepts the offer.
Ben Temalion enters the emperor's daughter, Rabbi Shimon exorcises him, they are allowed into the treasury, find the decree, and tear it up.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's testimony about the decree
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's testimony about the decree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi testifies that he saw the decree in Rome with drops of blood on it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi testifies that he saw the decree in Rome with drops of blood on it.

items.text: Mishnah: Non-combination of piggul and notar
items.text_en: Mishnah: Non-combination of piggul and notar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that piggul and notar do not combine because they are two different categories; similarly, a creeping thing and neveilah do not combine for impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that piggul (sacrifice rendered invalid by improper intent) and notar (leftover sacrificial meat) do not combine because they are two distinct categories; similarly, a creeping thing and neveilah do not combine for impurity, even by the lenient standard of either.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Yehuda's distinction on combination
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Yehuda's distinction on combination
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that the Mishnah's rule applies only to hand impurity (rabbinic), but for eating, they combine, as per Rabbi Eliezer's derivation from the verse.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the Mishnah's rule of non-combination applies only to hand impurity (טומאת ידיים), which is rabbinic.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes that for eating (אכילה), the items do combine to form a כזית (olive's bulk) for liability.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל כִּי קֹדֶשׁ הוּא' that anything invalidated in sanctity (including piggul and notar) carries a negative commandment for eating, supporting the combination for eating.

items.text: Mishnah: Combination of food impurities and measures
items.text_en: Mishnah: Combination of food impurities and measures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses combination of foods contaminated by different impurity levels, and lists various measures for different halachic contexts like eiruv, food impurity, Shabbat, and Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that food contaminated by an אב הטומאה (primary source of impurity) and food contaminated by a ולד הטומאה (secondary impurity) combine to convey impurity at the level of the lighter one.
The Mishnah adds that all foods combine to disqualify the body (פסול הגוויה) when they reach the measure of half a פרס (a loaf-sized volume).
The Mishnah lists various measures: two meals for עירוב (eiruv), an egg's bulk for food impurity, a dried fig's bulk for Shabbat carrying, and a date's bulk for Yom Kippur.
The Mishnah concludes that all liquids combine to disqualify the body at a quarter-לוג (log) measure, and at a mouthful (מלוא לוגמָא) for Yom Kippur.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon explains why foods combine: because a secondary impurity can become primary. The Gemara questions this, and Rava clarifies that the first causes the second; Rav Ashi adds that first and second are equivalent regarding a third.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that foods combine because a secondary impurity (שני) can become a primary impurity (ראשון).
The Gemara objects: can a secondary impurity actually become a primary impurity? That is impossible.
Rava clarifies: Rabbi Shimon means that the first impurity (ראשון) is what causes the second (שני), so they are linked.
Rav Ashi adds that first and second are equivalent regarding a third (שלישי), as they are both in the same category.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Orlah and Kil'ayim join
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Orlah and Kil'ayim join
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that orlah (fruit of a tree in its first three years) and kil'ayim (diverse seeds in a vineyard) join together to form the minimum measure for prohibition. Rabbi Shimon disagrees and says they do not join.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that orlah (fruit of a tree in its first three years) and kil'ayim (diverse seeds in a vineyard) join together to form the minimum measure for prohibition, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees and says they do not join.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon needs to say they do not join, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says any amount is enough for lashes. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah should read 'they do not need to join'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon would need to discuss joining at all, given his known position that any amount is significant for lashes.
The Gemara resolves by citing a baraita that Rabbi Shimon holds they do not need to join, meaning the Mishnah's statement is about a different point.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah should read 'they do not need to join' (אֵין צְרִיכִין לְצָרֵף), meaning Rabbi Shimon's statement is about necessity, not possibility.

items.text: Mishnah: Fabrics join for impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Fabrics join for impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that different materials like wool, sackcloth, leather, and matting join together for impurity. Rabbi Shimon explains the reason: they are all fit to become impure through sitting (midras impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that various materials (cloth, sack, leather, mat) join together for impurity, and Rabbi Shimon explains the reason is that they are all fit to become impure through sitting.
Rabbi Shimon explains the reason: all these materials are susceptible to טומאת מושב (impurity of sitting), so they join together.

items.text: Gemara: Minimum measures for fabrics
items.text_en: Gemara: Minimum measures for fabrics
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one cuts three handbreadths from various materials and makes a garment for lying, the minimum is three; for sitting, a handbreadth; for handling, any amount. Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai explains 'for handling' refers to a loom, and a baraita says it is for fig cutters.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches the minimum measures for fabrics used for lying (three handbreadths), sitting (a handbreadth), and handling (any amount).
The Gemara asks what 'for handling' means in the baraita.

sub.text: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai explains that 'for handling' refers to a loom (נַוְולָה).
A baraita adds that the fabric is fit for fig cutters (קוֹצְצֵי תְאֵנִים) to hold.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the formula 'Hadran alach' (we return to you), marking the end of the discussion on consecrated items of the altar.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula marking the end of the chapter on 'Sacred Items of the Altar'.

items.text: Mishnah: Benefiting from consecrated property
items.text_en: Mishnah: Benefiting from consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who benefits from consecrated property worth a perutah, even without causing damage, is liable for me'ilah according to Rabbi Akiva. The Sages distinguish: if the item can be damaged, liability requires damage; if not, benefit alone suffices. Examples are given for jewelry, drinking vessels, and tools.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Akiva's ruling that one who benefits from consecrated property worth a perutah is liable for me'ilah even without causing damage.
The Sages distinguish: for items that can be damaged, liability requires damage; for items that cannot be damaged, benefit alone suffices.
The Mishnah provides examples: jewelry and drinking vessels (no damage) trigger liability upon benefit; garments and tools (damage possible) require damage.
The Mishnah adds a special rule for a sin offering: while alive, liability requires damage; when dead, benefit alone suffices.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Sages
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva agrees with the Sages regarding items that can be damaged. Rava explains the dispute is about an intermediate garment and a 'malmela' (a type of tool or garment).

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Akiva concedes to the Sages regarding an item that can be damaged.
The Gemara asks: Since Rabbi Akiva agrees with the Sages on this point, over what do they actually disagree?
Rava answers that the dispute concerns an intermediate garment and a garment made of very thin fabric (מלמלא).

items.text: Derashah on the verse of me'ilah
items.text_en: Derashah on the verse of me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that expounds the word 'nefesh' in the verse to include an individual, a prince, and the anointed priest. It then explains that 'ma'al' means change, citing verses from Numbers and Chronicles.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the word 'נפש' (soul) in the verse to include an individual, a prince, and the anointed priest.
The baraita explains that 'מעל' (misuse) means change, citing verses from Numbers and Chronicles as proof.

items.text: Opening biblical citation
items.text_en: Opening biblical citation
items.desc_en: The daf begins with a verse from Hosea (2:7) about going after lovers, which serves as a prooftext for the concept of me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a biblical verse from Hosea (2:7) about going after lovers, serving as a prooftext for the concept of me'ilah.

items.text: Gezerah shavah from terumah to me'ilah
items.text_en: Gezerah shavah from terumah to me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether me'ilah applies when one damages without benefit or benefits without damage, and for attached items and agents. It answers with a gezerah shavah: just as 'chet' in terumah requires damage and benefit together, from detached items, and through an agent, so too in me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises possible cases for me'ilah: damaging without benefit, benefiting without damage, attached items, and an agent who performed his agency.
The Gemara introduces a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) from the word 'chet' in terumah to 'chet' in me'ilah.
The Gemara details the halakhot derived from terumah: damage and benefit together, same person, same item, simultaneously, detached items, and through an agent.
The Gemara applies the same halakhot to me'ilah via the gezerah shavah.

items.text: Expansion to eating without damage and combining actions
items.text_en: Expansion to eating without damage and combining actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about cases not covered by the analogy: eating without damage, combining one's own eating with another's, benefit with another's eating, etc., even over a long period. It derives these from the double expression 'tim'ol ma'al'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive liability for one who derives benefit from consecrated property without causing damage, which is not covered by the analogy to תרומה (priestly portion)?

The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that one's own consumption and another's consumption, or one's own benefit and another's benefit, or mixed cases, combine to the value of a פרוטה (peruta) even over a long period?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'תִּמְעֹל מַעַל' (if anyone commits a misuse) teaches that one is liable in any case, covering all these scenarios.

items.text: Combining two eating events over time
items.text_en: Combining two eating events over time
items.desc_en: The Gemara anticipates a possible limitation: just as terumah does not combine two separate eating events, so too me'ilah might not. It rejects this, deriving from 'tim'ol ma'al' that eating today and tomorrow, even over a long period, combine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: just as the word 'חטא' (sin) in the context of תרומה (priestly portion) does not combine two separate eating events into one, so too in מעילה (misuse of sacred property) it might not combine them.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that eating today and eating tomorrow, even over a long period, combine for מעילה?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'תִּמְעֹל מַעַל' (you commit a trespass) teaches that it combines in all cases, even over extended time.

items.text: Combining one's own eating with another's over years
items.text_en: Combining one's own eating with another's over years
items.desc_en: The Gemara further asks: just as terumah requires damage and benefit simultaneously, how do we know that one's own eating combines with another's eating, even over three years? It answers again from 'tim'ol ma'al'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: just as the 'חטא' (sin) stated regarding תרומה (priestly portion) requires damage and benefit simultaneously, from where do we derive that one's own eating combines with another's eating for מעילה (misuse of sacred property)?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'תִּמְעֹל מַעַל' (you shall commit a trespass) teaches that even eating over a span of three years combines, using the inclusive language 'מִכׇּל מָקוֹם' (in any case).

items.text: Incomplete derivation (daf continues)
items.text_en: Incomplete derivation (daf continues)
items.desc_en: The daf cuts off mid-sentence as the Gemara begins another 'i mah' objection, which will be completed on the next amud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins an objection (אִי מָה) comparing the term 'חטא' used in תרומה (priestly portion) to its use in מעילה (misuse of sacred property), but the daf cuts off mid-sentence.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Defining meilah for sacred-to-chullin transitions
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Defining meilah for sacred-to-chullin transitions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who takes a sacred item from the sacred domain to the chullin (non-sacred) domain commits meilah. It then specifies cases where the item moves from one sacred domain to another (e.g., buying bird offerings for zavim, bringing a sin-offering from the treasury) and debates when liability begins: Rabbi Shimon says upon removal, Rabbi Yehuda says until blood is sprinkled. The source is the verse 'tim'ol ma'al' (meilah) implying any removal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining meilah as taking a sacred item from the sacred domain to the chullin (non-sacred) domain.
The Mishnah lists cases of moving from one sacred domain to another, such as buying bird offerings for zavim or bringing a sin-offering from the treasury.
Rabbi Shimon rules that liability for meilah begins immediately upon removal from the sacred domain.
Rabbi Yehuda objects, holding that meilah liability is delayed until the blood is sprinkled on the altar.
The Mishnah cites the verse 'תִּמְעֹל מַעַל' (you shall commit meilah) to derive that any removal, even between sacred domains, constitutes meilah.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Who is included in 'nefesh' for meilah liability?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Who is included in 'nefesh' for meilah liability?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The verse 'nefesh' (soul) for meilah liability includes the unique individual, the prince, and the anointed one? It answers simply: 'nefesh' is written, so it includes all. But then it clarifies: The verse 'asher yiten mimenu al zar' (who gives from it to a stranger) excludes the anointed one because he is not a stranger (he is already anointed within). This teaches that the anointed one is exempt from meilah for giving sacred oil to another anointed one.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the word 'nefesh' in the verse includes the individual, the prince, and the anointed one.
The Gemara asks why this is necessary, since the word 'nefesh' is already written and obviously includes all.

The Gemara explains that without the inclusion, one might have thought the anointed one is exempt because the verse 'who gives from it to a stranger' excludes him, since he is not a stranger; therefore the verse teaches that he is included.

items.text: Gemara's analogies: Comparing meilah to sotah, idolatry, and terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's analogies: Comparing meilah to sotah, idolatry, and terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws analogies: Just as sotah (suspected adulteress) is liable even without physical damage (giving a ring), so too sacred items. Just as idolatry requires a change (breaking an idol) for liability, so too sacred items require damage (breaking with an axe). Just as terumah exempts a mere damager (one who eats without damaging), so too sacred items exempt a mere damager. These analogies refine the scope of meilah liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the analogies: just as sotah (suspected adulteress) is liable even without physical damage, so too sacred items are liable when one gives a ring.
The Gemara draws an analogy to idolatry: just as idolatry requires a change (breaking an idol) for liability, so too sacred items require damage (breaking with an axe).
The Gemara draws an analogy to תרומה (priestly portion): just as terumah exempts a mere damager (one who eats without damaging), so too sacred items exempt a mere damager.

items.text: Gemara's objection: Is gold exempt from meilah because it cannot be damaged?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Is gold exempt from meilah because it cannot be damaged?
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Zevid: Is gold exempt from meilah because it cannot be physically damaged? He points to the gold of Nun's daughter-in-law that went missing – where did it go? Rav Zevid answers: Perhaps it was the gold that was thrown to the daughter-in-law. And further: Even if there was no benefit or damage immediately, is there never any eventual damage? This challenges the exemption for gold.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's question to Rav Zevid
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's question to Rav Zevid
