sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Zevid: Is gold exempt from meilah because it cannot be damaged? He cites the gold of Nun's daughter-in-law that went missing as a counterexample.
Rav Zevid answers: Perhaps the missing gold was the gold thrown to the daughter-in-law. He further challenges: Even if there is no immediate benefit or damage, is there not eventual damage?

items.text: Gemara's conclusion: The case of benefiting from a sin-offering without damage
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion: The case of benefiting from a sin-offering without damage
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with the case of one who benefits from a sin-offering (e.g., eats it) without physically damaging it. Rav Papa clarifies: We are dealing with a blemished animal (a sin-offering with a defect), which is like a gold cup – it can be used without damage. This resolves the earlier objection about gold's exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of one who benefits from a sin-offering.
The Gemara objects: if the animal is unblemished, it is like the gold cup (which was exempt from me'ilah), so why would the Mishnah list it?
Rav Papa resolves the difficulty: the Mishnah deals with a blemished sin-offering, which can be used without damage, analogous to the gold cup.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules of me'ilah and multiple offenders
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules of me'ilah and multiple offenders
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one derives benefit of half a perutah and damages half a perutah, or derives benefit of a perutah from one item and damages a perutah from another, he has not committed me'ilah. It then rules that multiple successive acts of me'ilah apply only to an animal and a service vessel, giving examples of riding an animal, drinking from a gold cup, and plucking from a chatat offering. Rabbi adds that anything without redemption has multiple me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule that one is not liable for me'ilah unless both benefit and damage reach a perutah from the same item.
The Mishnah states that multiple successive acts of me'ilah apply only to an animal and a service vessel.
The Mishnah gives examples: riding an animal, drinking from a gold cup, and plucking from a chatat offering, each with multiple successive users.
Rabbi adds that anything without redemption has multiple me'ilah.

items.text: Gemara identifies the Mishnah's author and explains the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara identifies the Mishnah's author and explains the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, answering it is Rabbi Nechemya, as a beraita states: The Tanna Kamma says multiple me'ilah applies only to an animal, while Rabbi Nechemya says animal and service vessel. The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's reasoning: the verse about me'ilah is written in the context of a ram of guilt-offering. Rabbi Nechemya uses a kal vachomer argument: if others (non-sacred items) bring an animal into sanctity, then the animal itself certainly does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah and identifies it as Rabbi Nechemya.
A baraita is cited: the first Tanna says multiple me'ilah applies only to an animal, while Rabbi Nechemya says animal and service vessel.
The Gemara explains the first Tanna's reasoning: the matter of an animal is written in the verse about the ram of the guilt-offering.
Rabbi Nechemya argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if other items bring their own sanctity, then an animal itself certainly does.

items.text: Rava distinguishes between Rabbi and Tanna Kamma regarding wood
items.text_en: Rava distinguishes between Rabbi and Tanna Kamma regarding wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi's statement in the Mishnah seems identical to the Tanna Kamma. Rava says the difference between them is wood: whether wood used as a sacrifice is subject to multiple me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi's statement in the Mishnah differs from the Tanna Kamma, since it appears identical.
Rava answers that the difference between Rabbi and the Tanna Kamma concerns wood (whether wood used as a sacrifice is subject to multiple me'ilah).

items.text: Supporting beraita and further statements about wood
items.text_en: Supporting beraita and further statements about wood
items.desc_en: A beraita is cited: one who vows to bring wood must bring at least two logs. Rabbi says wood is a sacrifice, requiring salt and waving. Rava then says according to Rabbi, wood requires wood (for fuel), and Rav Pappa says according to Rabbi, wood requires kemitzah (handful removal).

sub.desc_en: A beraita is cited: one who vows to bring wood must bring at least two logs; Rabbi says wood is a sacrifice requiring salt and waving.
Rava states that according to Rabbi, wood (as a sacrifice) requires wood (for fuel).
Rav Pappa adds that according to Rabbi, wood requires קְמִיצָה (handful removal).

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative distinction: blemished sacrifices
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative distinction: blemished sacrifices
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers another difference between Rabbi and the Tanna Kamma: unblemished Temple offerings that became blemished and were slaughtered. A beraita states Rabbi says they are buried, while the Sages say they are redeemed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers a different difference: sanctified animals that were blemished and then slaughtered — whether they are buried or redeemed.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi says such animals are buried, while the Sages say they are redeemed.
The baraita concludes with the Sages' ruling that the animals are redeemed.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah: taking a stone or beam
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah: taking a stone or beam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new topic: one who takes a consecrated stone or beam has not committed me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens a new topic: one who takes a stone or beam from consecrated property has not committed me'ilah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of me'ilah with a sukakh and a prutah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of me'ilah with a sukakh and a prutah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases: one who builds a sukakh from hekdesh wood is not liable until he dwells under it worth a prutah; one who takes a prutah of hekdesh is not liable until he gives it to another; giving it to a bathhouse attendant causes immediate liability even without bathing. The Mishnah concludes that various combinations of eating and deriving benefit from hekdesh combine to form the measure for liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who gives a sukakh to another is liable for me'ilah, but the recipient is not, and one who builds a sukakh in his house is not liable until he dwells under it worth a prutah.
The Mishnah adds that one who takes a prutah of hekdesh is not liable until he gives it to another, and giving it to a bathhouse attendant causes immediate liability even without bathing.
The Mishnah concludes that various combinations of eating and deriving benefit from hekdesh combine to form the measure for liability.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why distinguish between him and his friend?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why distinguish between him and his friend?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the one who takes the prutah and his friend regarding liability. Shmuel answers that we are dealing with a treasurer who is entrusted with the funds, so his friend is not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the giver and the recipient regarding liability for me'ilah.
Shmuel answers that the Mishnah deals with a treasurer (גזבר) who has items entrusted to him, so the giver is liable for misusing hekdesh but the recipient is not.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Why no liability until dwelling under the sukakh?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Why no liability until dwelling under the sukakh?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one is not liable immediately upon building the sukakh, since he changed it. Rav answers that it is like placing it on an opening (so it is not yet a dwelling). The Gemara then discusses whether building alone causes liability, citing Rav's statement that bowing to a house prohibits it. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that visible benefit is prohibited by the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one is not liable for מעילה (misuse of consecrated property) until he dwells under the sukakh, since building it already constitutes a change.
Rav answers that the case is where he placed the sukakh on an opening, so it is not yet a dwelling and no benefit is derived.
The Gemara suggests that once he builds the sukakh, he should still be liable for מעילה (misuse) because the building itself is a benefit.
The Gemara cites Rav's principle that bowing to a house prohibits it, suggesting that building alone might cause liability.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika resolves that the Torah only prohibits visible benefit (הנאה הניראת לעינים), and building alone does not constitute such benefit.

items.text: Discussion: Dwelling in a consecrated house and the distinction of timing
items.text_en: Discussion: Dwelling in a consecrated house and the distinction of timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a support from the case of one who dwells in a consecrated house and is liable. Reish Lakish distinguishes: if one consecrated it and then built it, liability applies; but if one built it and then consecrated it, there is no liability. The Gemara questions why the Tanna didn't teach the case of a stone house built and then consecrated. The answer is that the case is where the roof is not fixed (פסיקא) versus where it is fixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that a baraita about one who dwells in a consecrated house and is liable supports Rav's opinion that a detached item retains its status when attached.
Reish Lakish rejects the support, explaining that the baraita deals with a case where one consecrated the materials first and then built the house, so misuse applies even after attachment.
The Gemara questions: if one built the house and then consecrated it, is the dweller exempt from misuse?
The Gemara objects: why did the tanna run to teach the case of a cave house? Let him teach the case of a stone house built and then consecrated, which would also be exempt.
The Gemara suggests that the tanna could have simply stated the case of a stone house built and then consecrated, which would also be exempt.
The Gemara resolves: the case of a cave is conclusive (פסיקא) — always exempt — while a stone house is not conclusive, as it depends on whether the materials were consecrated before building.
The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the standard phrase 'הדרן עלך הנהנה' (we return to you, chapter 'The one who benefits').

items.text: Mishnah: The shaliach who performs or deviates from his mission
items.text_en: Mishnah: The shaliach who performs or deviates from his mission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if a shaliach performs his mission, the homeowner is liable for me'ilah; if not, the shaliach is liable. Examples: if told to give meat and gave liver, or vice versa, the shaliach is liable. If told to give one piece and he says take two, and they take three, all are liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: if the agent performed his agency properly, the homeowner is liable for misuse; if not, the agent is liable.
The Mishnah provides examples: if told to give meat and gave liver, or vice versa, the agent is liable; if told to give one piece and he says take two and they take three, all are liable.

items.text: Gemara's opening question
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that any matter where the messenger has discretion constitutes two separate acts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that any matter where the messenger has discretion constitutes two separate acts.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Abaye's dispute over the Tanna
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Abaye's dispute over the Tanna
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Akiva, who forbids gourds in a vow from vegetables. Abaye argues that even Rabbi Akiva would require consultation, and Rava supports Abaye's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that the Mishnah's Tanna is not Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva forbids gourds in a vow from vegetables.
Abaye objects that even Rabbi Akiva would require consultation, as the agent must ask the sender.
Rava supports Abaye's view, declaring that Nachmani (Abaye) spoke well.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits head, feet, and other parts in a vow from meat, and states that innards are not meat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna disagrees with Rabbi Akiva regarding the definition of meat.
The Gemara identifies Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits head, feet, and other parts in a vow from meat.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that innards (קְרָבַיִים) are not considered meat, and one who eats them is not considered a proper person.

items.text: Gemara's challenge on fish vs. fowl
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge on fish vs. fowl
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first Tanna distinguishes fowl from fish, given that people might say they couldn't find animal meat and brought fish instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first Tanna distinguishes fowl from fish, and challenges that the same reasoning (one cannot find meat of land animals) would apply to fish as well.

items.text: Rav Papa's first answer and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav Papa's first answer and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Papa answers that we deal with a day of bloodletting when one does not eat fish. The Gemara objects that fowl is also avoided then, citing Shmuel and a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa answers that the Mishnah deals with a day of bloodletting (הקזה), when one does not eat fish.

The Gemara objects that if so, fowl should also be avoided, citing Shmuel's statement that eating fowl after bloodletting makes the heart flutter, and a baraita that one should not let blood after eating fish, fowl, or salted meat.

items.text: Rav Papa's second answer
items.text_en: Rav Papa's second answer
items.desc_en: Rav Papa revises his answer, saying we deal with a day when one's eyes hurt, and then one does not eat fish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa revises his answer: we are dealing with a day when one's eye hurts, and one does not eat fish.

items.text: Proof that adding to instructions makes one a messenger
items.text_en: Proof that adding to instructions makes one a messenger
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's case that adding to one's instructions still constitutes a valid agency. Rav Sheshet explains that the messenger said he took one piece according to the sender's intent and one according to his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's case that adding to one's instructions still constitutes a valid agency.
Rav Sheshet explains that the messenger said he took one piece according to the sender's intent and one according to his own, thus the agency is valid.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's first case
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's first case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that mental reservations are not legally effective; the owner is liable even if he intended a different window.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah teaches that mental reservations are not legally effective; the owner is liable even if he intended a different window.

items.text: Mishnah: Agency and me'ilah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Agency and me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where an agent deviates from instructions, determining liability for me'ilah. It also discusses agents who are deaf-mute, insane, or minors, and the procedure for redeeming consecrated items.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case where the agent brought from the same general location as instructed, and the homeowner is liable for me'ilah even if he mentally intended a different specific spot.
The Mishnah presents a contrasting case where the agent deviated from the explicit location instruction, making the agent liable for me'ilah.
The Mishnah rules that when an agent is a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor, the homeowner is liable if the agent carried out the mission, but the storekeeper is liable if the agent did not.
The Mishnah rules that if a competent agent remembers the consecrated status before reaching the storekeeper, the storekeeper is liable for me'ilah when he later uses the item.
The Mishnah concludes with the procedure for redeeming consecrated items by using a perutah or vessel, stating that consecrated property can be redeemed with money or its equivalent.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's first ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's first ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah teaches, and answers that it teaches that mental reservations are not legally significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel teaching the Mishnah's first ruling conveys.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that mental reservations (דברים שבלב) are not legally significant.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on agents who are deaf-mute, insane, or minors
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on agents who are deaf-mute, insane, or minors
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how such individuals can be agents, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan offer explanations based on analogous cases from other tractates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor can serve as an agent for מעילה (misuse of consecrated property), since they are not legally capable of agency.

Rabbi Elazar answers that the mishnah treats these agents like the minimal pressing of olives (מעטן של זיתים), citing a baraita about when olives become susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity) to show that even minimal action suffices.

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different answer, comparing the case to a mishnah about עירוב (eruv) where an animal carries the eruv, showing that the agent's action is considered effective even without full legal capacity.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the agent who forgets
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the agent who forgets
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita regarding who is liable when the owner remembers but the agent does not. Rav Sheshet resolves it by explaining the Mishnah refers to when both remember.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says the agent is exempt even if not reminded, but a baraita says the agent is liable if only the owner remembered.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's case is when both the owner and the agent remembered.

items.text: Mishnah: Further cases of agency and me'ilah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Further cases of agency and me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents additional cases involving partial deviation from instructions, including when the agent buys different items or uses money for unintended purposes, and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: if the owner gave a perutah and instructed the agent to buy half candles and half wicks, but the agent bought all of one type, neither party is liable for me'ilah.
The Mishnah adds a second case: if the owner specified locations for each item and the agent swapped locations, the agent is liable for me'ilah.
The Tanna Kamma rules that when the owner gave two perutot for an etrog and the agent bought an etrog with one and a pomegranate with the other, both parties are liable for me'ilah.
Rabbi Yehuda disputes, arguing that the owner is not liable because he can claim he wanted a large etrog and received a small, poor one.
The Mishnah introduces a final case: the owner gave a gold dinar and instructed the agent to bring a cloak.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Agency and Meilah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Agency and Meilah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where an agent buys a cloak and a tallit for three coins each, and both parties are liable for meilah. Rabbi Yehuda exempts the homeowner because he can claim he wanted a large cloak.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when an agent buys a cloak and a tallit for three coins each, both parties are liable for meilah, but Rabbi Yehuda exempts the homeowner because he can claim he wanted a large cloak.

items.text: Gemara's Question on Agency and Acquisition
items.text_en: Gemara's Question on Agency and Acquisition
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one tells an agent to buy a kor of land and he buys a litkha, the buyer acquires it. It clarifies the case as one where the agent brought goods worth six for three. Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is explained: the homeowner can say he would have paid more for a better item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one tells an agent to buy a kor of land and he buys a litkha, the buyer acquires it.
The Gemara clarifies the case as one where the agent brought goods worth six for three dinars.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yehuda's statement that the homeowner did not misuse consecrated property.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the homeowner can say he would have paid more for a better item.

items.text: Support from the Seifa and Rav Pappa's Resolution
items.text_en: Support from the Seifa and Rav Pappa's Resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara finds support from the seifa where Rabbi Yehuda concedes in the case of small beans that both parties are liable, because beans are sold per unit. Rav Pappa explains that in a place where items are sold by count, the price is fixed, so the agent's deviation is not grounds for rejection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that it is reasonable, citing the seifa where Rabbi Yehuda concedes in the case of small beans that both parties are liable because beans are sold per unit.
The Gemara questions the scenario: if items are sold by appraisal, even for beans the seller would discount a larger payment, so why would both be liable?
Rav Pappa resolves that the case is in a place where items are sold by count (כַּנֵּי כַּנֵּי), so the price is fixed and the agent's deviation is not grounds for rejection.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Depositing Money with a Money-Changer or Homeowner
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Depositing Money with a Money-Changer or Homeowner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between depositing money with a money-changer (if tied, not to be used; if loose, may be used) and with a homeowner (never to be used). It also discusses a case where a consecrated perutah falls into one's purse, with a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for depositing money with a money-changer: if bound, he may not use it and is liable if he spends it; if loose, he may use it and is exempt.
The Mishnah states that with a homeowner, whether bound or loose, he may not use the money and is liable if he spends it.
Rabbi Meir rules that a storekeeper is like a homeowner.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a storekeeper is like a money-changer.
Rabbi Akiva rules that if a consecrated perutah falls into one's purse or one says 'a perutah in this purse is consecrated,' once he spends the first coin he is liable for misuse.
The Sages rule that he is not liable until he spends all the coins in the purse.
Rabbi Akiva concedes to the Sages that if one says 'a perutah from this purse is consecrated,' he may continue spending until he spends all the coins.

items.text: Gemara's Contradiction and Resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's Contradiction and Resolution
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan why the first part of the Mishnah (consecrated perutah in a purse) differs from the latter part (declaring 'one of my oxen'). Rabbi Yochanan answers that the latter case involves saying 'this purse shall not be free from consecration.' Ravin reports a similar question about oxen, with the same answer.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan why the first clause of the Mishnah (consecrated perutah in a purse) differs from the latter clause (declaring 'one of my oxen').
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the latter clause refers to one who said 'this purse shall not be free from consecration,' meaning the last coin is consecrated.

Ravin reports that Reish Lakish raised a similar contradiction between the Mishnah here and the Mishnah about bulls, and Rabbi Yochanan gave the same answer about the purse not being free from consecration.

items.text: Rav Pappa's comparison
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's comparison
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa compares the case of consecrated bags to the Mishnah about buying wine from Kutim, citing the Mishnah where one designates terumah and tithes from purchased wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa compares the case of consecrated bags to the Mishnah about buying wine from Kutim, citing the Mishnah where one designates terumah and tithes from purchased wine.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid the practice, contradicting Rav Pappa's comparison.
Rav Pappa answers that the end of the Mishnah refers to a case where one says 'this bag shall not be released from consecration,' explaining the dispute.

items.text: Objection from the other rabbis
items.text_en: Objection from the other rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon prohibit the practice described in the Mishnah, creating a contradiction to Rav Pappa's comparison.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon prohibit the practice, contradicting Rav Pappa's comparison.

items.text: Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the latter part of the Mishnah refers to a case where one says 'this bag shall not be exempt from consecration,' thereby resolving the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the latter part of the Mishnah refers to a case where one says 'this bag shall not be exempt from consecration,' thereby distinguishing it from the wine case.
